feedback.fine: The schema says `status` is a string — it doesn't say what strings are valid. `"closed"`, `"Closed"`, `"resolved"`, and `"done"` are all equally plausible guesses from the schema alone, and only one of them (if any) matches what your backend actually checks for.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Two things are missing: what values `status` actually accepts (an enum in the schema would fix this — lesson three), and which of the two overlapping tools to use when. "Updates a ticket" tells the model that a function exists; it doesn't tell it anything it needs to call that function correctly.

contentSections.body: The description isn't documentation for a developer who can go read the code — it's the entire interface the model has, re-read fresh on every decision, and anything it doesn't say gets guessed rather than left blank.

contentSections.title: What goes in the description that actually earns its place

contentSections.body: "Send a Slack message" is a description. "Post a message to a Slack channel. Use for status updates and notifications visible to a team; do not use for anything containing customer PII, which must go through send_secure_notification instead" is an interface — one sentence longer, and it's the sentence that prevents the one mistake that actually matters.

contentSections.problem: You're writing the description for a `create_calendar_event` tool in an agent that manages a team's shared calendar. Build the description from nothing.

steps.label: Start with what it does, plainly
steps.work: "Creates an event on the team's shared Google Calendar."
steps.why: This is necessary but, as lesson one's concept-flow showed, nowhere near sufficient on its own — it's the name restated in a sentence.

steps.label: Add when to use it versus not
steps.work: "Use this to schedule meetings, deadlines, or blocked focus time. Do not use this for one-off reminders only relevant to a single person — use create_personal_reminder for those."
steps.why: There's almost certainly a similarly-named tool nearby (a personal reminder tool, a task tool) and the model needs a rule for picking between them, not just two descriptions it has to compare and infer a boundary from.

steps.label: Add the consequence of getting it wrong
steps.work: "Events created here are visible to the whole team and trigger a notification to all invitees immediately."
steps.why: This is the sentence that changes behavior. Without it, an agent testing something might create a throwaway event and accidentally notify twelve people. Naming the blast radius is often more useful than naming the mechanics.

steps.label: Note any real-world constraint
steps.work: "Subject to Google Calendar API rate limits (typically 500 requests per 100 seconds per user) — if creating many events in a batch, expect this to be the bottleneck."
steps.why: The architecture guide's honesty rule applies to tool descriptions too: if a dependency has a real limit or cost, the agent benefits from knowing it exists, the same way a human colleague would want to know before batch-creating 800 events.

faded.problem: Now write the description for a `refund_order` tool, same procedure, for an agent that handles customer support tickets and has a separate `issue_store_credit` tool for smaller goodwill gestures.

blanks.prompt: Write the plain 'what it does' sentence.
blanks.answer: Issues a refund to the customer's original payment method for a specific order.
accept: refunds an order to the original payment method

blanks.prompt: Write the 'when to use this versus the other tool' sentence, naming the boundary.
blanks.answer: Use for confirmed order problems (wrong item, damaged goods, never arrived); use issue_store_credit instead for goodwill gestures with no confirmed order defect.
accept: use this for actual order problems, use issue_store_credit for goodwill without a defect

blanks.answer: This immediately charges the refund to the company's payment processor and cannot be reversed through this tool once submitted.
accept: it's an irreversible real charge back to the customer, no undo

faded.why: Refunds are higher-stakes than calendar events, which is exactly why the consequence sentence matters even more here — but the procedure for writing the description doesn't change based on stakes, only how much weight that third sentence needs to carry.

contentSections.procedure: Write, in order: (1) what it does in plain language, (2) when to use it and — critically — when to use a different tool instead, naming that tool, (3) what happens if it's called, especially anything visible, costly, or irreversible, (4) any real constraint (rate limit, cost, availability) worth knowing before calling it.

contentSections.body: A description earns its place with four things: what it does, when to use it instead of a similar tool, what happens when it's called, and any real-world constraint — and the second and third are the ones people skip, which is exactly why they're the ones worth checking for.

title: Writing a description that prevents misuse
description: Writing for the specific wrong call a model is likely to make — the near-duplicate tool, the plausible-but-wrong argument, the destructive action tried on a whim — rather than writing generically thorough documentation.

learningObjectives.text: Predict the specific wrong call a given tool description invites
Rewrite a tool description to close off a specific predicted misuse

contentSections.title: Writing against the mistake you can predict

contentSections.body: An agent with a `delete_branch` tool and a task to "clean up merged branches" deletes `main` on its second run, because someone had merged a PR *into* `main` earlier that day, and "merged branch" was ambiguous between "a branch that has been merged into something" and "a branch that other things have been merged into." The fix wasn't a smarter model. It was one clause in the description.

contentSections.scenario: The `delete_branch` tool's description read: "Deletes a git branch by name. Input: branch_name (string)." The agent, asked to clean up merged branches, called it with branch_name="main".
contentSections.question: What's the mechanism that let this happen, specifically?

options.label: "Merged branch" is genuinely ambiguous, and nothing in the tool or the task disambiguated it in the direction that matters
The model doesn't understand what a git branch is
The schema should have required a confirmation flag

feedback.ambiguous: Right. "Branches that have been merged into main" and "main, which things get merged into" both satisfy a loose reading of "merged branch" if you're not paying close attention to direction — and a model working through a list of branch names quickly, without a strong signal that main is categorically off-limits, can genuinely land on the wrong reading.
feedback.understand: The model understands git branches fine in isolation — ask it to explain what a merge is and it'll do so correctly. The failure isn't a knowledge gap, it's that the specific task phrasing had a plausible wrong reading and nothing closed that reading off.
feedback.confirm: A confirmation step is a reasonable second layer of defense (and often a good idea for destructive tools generally), but it doesn't fix the actual mechanism here — it just adds a chance to catch the mistake after it's already been decided on, rather than preventing the ambiguous reading from being reached at all.

contentSections.mechanism: A destructive tool with a generic description leaves the model to resolve ambiguity in the task itself, and ambiguity resolved under time/token pressure tends to resolve toward whatever reading is closer at hand — not necessarily the safe one.

contentSections.body:
The useful skill here is specific, not general: before shipping a tool description, name the *one* wrong call a model would plausibly make with it, and write a clause that closes exactly that door. "Be thorough" doesn't do this — thoroughness spreads attention evenly across a hundred things that were never going to go wrong and misses the one that was.

For `delete_branch`, the predictable mistake is deleting a protected branch. The fix: "Never delete `main`, `master`, `develop`, or any branch matching `release/*` — if asked to clean these up, refuse and explain why." That's not generic safety language, it's a specific, named list closing a specific, predicted hole.

A reliable way to find the hole: imagine the tool being called by someone junior, moving fast, from a task description that's slightly underspecified — which the vast majority of real task descriptions are. What's the first wrong thing they'd try? That's the sentence your description is missing.

Don't write a description to be generically thorough — predict the one specific wrong call this tool invites, given how it's likely to be asked for, and write the clause that closes exactly that door.

contentSections.title: The near-duplicate tool problem

contentSections.body: `send_message` and `send_notification` sit side by side in a tool list. Nobody wrote either description with the other one in mind. An agent asked to "let the on-call engineer know" now has a coin flip's worth of guidance for which one is correct, and picks whichever one's description happened to load a slightly more relevant-sounding synonym.

contentSections.scenario: An agent has three tools: `send_message` (posts to a Slack channel), `send_notification` (triggers a PagerDuty alert), and `send_email`. It's asked to "let the on-call engineer know the deploy failed."
contentSections.question: Which of these description fixes would actually resolve the ambiguity between the three tools — not just make each description individually longer?

items.label: Each description explicitly says when to prefer it over the other two, by name

send_notification's description states it should be used for anything requiring immediate, interruptive attention (it pages someone, possibly waking them up); the other two explicitly should not be used for urgent issues
Making each description longer and more detailed, without cross-referencing the other tools
Adding one example use case to each description that's genuinely distinct from the other tools' example use cases

explanation.cross: This directly attacks the actual problem — the ambiguity isn't within any one tool's description, it's in the gap *between* them. A description can be perfect in isolation and still leave the boundary between it and its neighbor completely unspecified.
explanation.urgency: This is the real fix for this specific case: the distinguishing fact isn't the medium (Slack vs. page vs. email), it's urgency and interruption cost, and naming that explicitly gives the model the actual decision criterion rather than three descriptions of mechanism.
explanation.longer: More detail on what each tool does mechanically doesn't touch the actual gap. You can describe Slack-posting in exhaustive detail and still leave 'versus PagerDuty, when' completely unanswered.
explanation.examples: A genuinely distinct example per tool (e.g. send_notification's example is 'production is down,' send_message's is 'the daily standup summary is ready') gives the model something to pattern-match the current situation against, which is a real and different signal from a mechanical description.

contentSections.synthesis: Near-duplicate tools fail not because any one description is bad, but because the boundary between them was never written down anywhere. The fix is always relational — each tool's description should name its neighbors and say what specifically routes to it instead of them.

contentSections.body: When two tools are plausible for the same request, the fix isn't a longer description of either one in isolation — it's naming the boundary between them explicitly, in both descriptions, using the actual criterion that should decide it.

title: Parameters, schemas and the argument it invents
description: Using JSON Schema constraints — enums, required fields, types, descriptions on individual parameters — to make the wrong argument value structurally hard to produce, not just discouraged in prose.

learningObjectives.text: Use enum, required, and type constraints to narrow the space of arguments a model can construct
Diagnose a hallucinated-argument failure back to a specific missing schema constraint

contentSections.title: The schema is a fence, not a suggestion

contentSections.body: A `set_priority` tool's schema says `{"priority": {"type": "string"}}`. Across a hundred real calls, the model sends `"high"`, `"High"`, `"P1"`, `"urgent"`, and once, memorably, `"as soon as possible"` — five different strings for what was, in the backend, exactly three valid values. None of these are the model being careless. Every one of them is a reasonable guess at a value the schema never actually specified.

contentSections.question: Two structural problems in this schema, beyond the vague description from lesson one — what are they?

options.label: priority has no enum constraining it to valid values, and required isn't set on ticket_id, so a call missing it is technically schema-valid
The tool needs a description on priority, but the top-level schema is otherwise fine
input_schema should use "type": "array" instead of "type": "object"

feedback.both: Right, and they compound: with no `enum`, `priority` can be any string the model considers plausible — Sentence case, abbreviations, whole phrases. With no `required` array, a call with `ticket_id` omitted validates against this schema just fine, and your backend finds out it's missing only when it actually tries to use it, several steps later than you'd want to catch it.
feedback.desc-only: A per-parameter description on `priority` (e.g. listing the valid values in prose) would help, but a JSON Schema `enum` does something a description can't: it makes an invalid value a validation error the client-side tooling can reject before the call ever reaches your code, not just a value your backend has to notice is wrong after the fact.
feedback.array: Tool arguments are a set of named parameters, which is exactly what `"type": "object"` with a `properties` map represents — an array wouldn't have named fields like `ticket_id` and `priority` at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: `"type": "string"` with no `enum` describes an unbounded space — any string satisfies it. `enum: ["low", "medium", "high"]` shrinks that space to exactly three values; the model isn't discouraged from sending something else, it's structurally unable to produce a schema-valid call with anything else. That's the difference between a fence and a sign asking people not to cross.

contentSections.body: A description tells the model what a value means; a schema constraint (enum, required, type, pattern) makes the wrong value structurally impossible to send — use both, because they close different holes.

contentSections.title: When the model invents a plausible-looking value anyway

contentSections.body: A `get_weather` tool takes a `zip_code` field, correctly typed as a string, correctly required. The model calls it with `zip_code: "downtown Seattle"` — schema-valid (it's a string, it's present) and completely wrong, because the user said "downtown Seattle" and the model passed the phrase straight through rather than resolving it to an actual ZIP code, because nothing told it that resolution was its job rather than the tool's.

contentSections.scenario: A team adds a `pattern` regex constraining `zip_code` to `^\d{5}$` and reruns the same 30 test prompts (a mix of "in Seattle," "98101," "near the Space Needle") that previously produced free-text location guesses about a third of the time.
contentSections.question: After adding the regex pattern alone — no other change — roughly what fraction of those 30 runs now produce a genuinely correct 5-digit ZIP code on the first call?
contentSections.explanation: A pattern constraint stops the model from sending something that obviously fails validation, but it doesn't teach the model how to *resolve* "downtown Seattle" into 98101 — that's a lookup the model can't do from the regex alone. In practice teams see the pattern catch and reject some free-text guesses (which the model then often retries correctly, or errors out on), but it doesn't fix cases where the model needed a genuinely different piece of information, like a geocoding step, before it could produce a valid ZIP at all. The real fix here usually isn't a tighter schema on this tool — it's a separate `geocode_location` tool the model can call first, feeding its output into `get_weather`.

contentSections.body: This is the limit of what a schema alone can do, and it's worth stating plainly: a schema constrains the *shape* of a value, never whether the model has the information to produce the *right* one. `pattern: "^\\d{5}$"` will reject `"downtown Seattle"` — good — but it can't manufacture a correct ZIP code out of a location the model was never given a way to resolve. When you see a model reliably producing schema-valid but *substantively* wrong arguments, the fix usually isn't a tighter schema on the same tool; it's recognizing that this tool needs an input the model doesn't have, and giving it a way to get one — another tool, a lookup, a piece of context passed in earlier. Schema tightening fixes format problems. Missing-tool problems need another tool.
A schema constraint fixes the shape of a bad argument; it can't fix the model not having the information to construct a correct one — that's a missing-tool problem, not a missing-constraint problem.

title: Return values the model can act on
description: What a tool hands back matters as much as what it accepts — a return value the model can parse, reason from, and act on differently depending on what happened, versus a dump that leaves the model guessing at what succeeded.

learningObjectives.text: Design a tool return value that lets the model distinguish success, empty result, and failure without guessing
Identify when a raw API/database response is unusable as a tool return value

contentSections.title: What comes back is also an interface

contentSections.body: A `search_orders` tool returns an empty JSON array, `[]`, when there are no matching orders. It also returns `[]` when the search itself failed silently because the customer ID was malformed. Both cases print identically to the model as "no results," and on both, the agent confidently tells the customer "we found no orders matching that description" — which is true in one case and a masked bug in the other.

contentSections.scenario: The agent told a customer their order history was empty. In fact, the search silently failed on a malformed customer ID and the backend logged an error the agent's tool call never saw.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind the wrong answer?

options.label: The tool's return value collapsed two different situations (no results, and a failed lookup) into the same shape
The model should have double-checked with a second search before answering
The customer gave a malformed ID, so this is a user-input problem, not a tool problem

feedback.collapse: Right. `[]` is structurally identical whether it means 'searched successfully, zero matches' or 'the search never actually ran.' The model has no information in the return value that would let it tell these apart, so it can't distinguish them even if it wanted to — the return value itself destroyed the distinction before the model ever saw it.
feedback.double-check: Asking the model to 'just double-check' treats a design problem as a diligence problem. Even a maximally careful model can't distinguish two situations that produce byte-identical output — there's nothing in `[]` to notice is suspicious, because it's a completely valid response to a real empty search too.
feedback.user-fault: The malformed ID is where the chain started, but the tool's job is to fail *loudly* on a malformed input it can't process, not to silently return the same empty result it would for a legitimate zero-match search. A tool that swallows an internal error and returns an empty-but-successful-looking shape is the actual defect here.

contentSections.mechanism: A return value that can't distinguish 'nothing found' from 'something went wrong' forces the model to treat both as the same case — and it will, confidently, because from where it's sitting they genuinely look the same.

contentSections.body: A tool result has to let the model tell apart 'succeeded with nothing to report' from 'failed' — collapse those into the same shape and the model can't distinguish them either, no matter how carefully it reads.

contentSections.title: Too much information is its own failure

contentSections.body: A `get_customer` tool returns the full database row — 40 fields, including internal flags, a raw audit-log blob, and three deprecated columns nobody's cleaned up. The model, asked to check whether a customer's email is verified, has to find one boolean buried in forty fields of noise, every single time it calls this tool, on every agent that ever uses it.

contentSections.problem: Redesign `get_customer`'s return value so an agent checking email-verification status can actually use it efficiently.

steps.label: Identify what's actually needed for the common case
steps.work: The task at hand needs: name, email, whether it's verified, and account status. Not: internal risk-scoring flags, raw timestamps in three formats, a legacy billing ID nobody references anymore.
steps.why: A tool return isn't a database dump — it's an answer to 'what does the model need to know to do the next thing,' and most tasks need a small slice of a large row.

steps.label: Trim to that slice by default
steps.work: {"name": ..., "email": ..., "email_verified": true, "account_status": "active"}
steps.why: Fewer fields means fewer tokens (which the model re-reads on every subsequent turn, per module 1's point about the array growing) and a much shorter path to the one field that actually mattered.

steps.label: Offer the rest as an option, not a default
steps.work: Add an optional `include_full_record: bool` parameter to the tool's input schema, defaulting to false, for the rarer case that genuinely needs everything.
steps.why: This keeps the common case cheap and fast without making the rare case impossible — the model can ask for more when it actually needs more, instead of always paying for the maximum.

steps.label: Keep field names self-explanatory
steps.work: email_verified rather than a bare flag named ev_flag or status_3.
steps.why: The model is reading these field names the same way it reads the description — a cryptic name is a small version of the same vague-description problem from lesson one.

blanks.prompt: What's the minimal slice of information this task actually needs?
blanks.answer: Whether the deploy succeeded, when it ran, and — if it failed — the specific error, not the full log.
accept: success/fail status, timestamp, and the failure reason if any

blanks.prompt: What should happen to the hundreds of lines of raw build log by default?
blanks.answer: They should be left out of the default response entirely, available only via an optional parameter or a separate tool for deeper investigation.

blanks.answer: Every extra token in the tool result gets re-sent and re-billed on every subsequent turn of the loop, and buries the one fact (pass/fail) the model actually needs to find.

contentSections.procedure: 1. Name the specific question this tool call is usually answering. 2. Trim the return value to what actually answers it. 3. Make anything beyond that optional, not default. 4. Use field names that are self-explanatory without cross-referencing documentation.

contentSections.body: A tool result stuffed with everything the backend has isn't more helpful, it's a haystack — return the slice that answers the question this call is usually asking, and make the rest opt-in.

title: Too many tools, and the choice that gets worse
description: Why tool-selection accuracy degrades as the tool list grows, even when every individual description is well-written — and the real fixes (grouping, staged exposure, retrieval) versus the fake ones (just write better descriptions).

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a long tool list degrades selection accuracy even with good individual descriptions
Choose an appropriate mitigation (grouping, staging, retrieval) for a given tool-count problem

contentSections.title: More tools, worse choices — even good ones

contentSections.body: A team builds an internal ops agent, adds a tool every time someone needs a new capability, and eighteen months later it has 60 well-documented, individually well-written tools. Tool-selection accuracy — did it call the right one — has quietly dropped from something like 95% to somewhere in the 70s, and not one individual tool description got worse in that time.

contentSections.scenario: A controlled comparison: the same model, the same task set, given first 8 tools and then 45 tools (all well-described, all individually reasonable), on tasks that only ever need one of the first 8.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many percentage points does correct-tool-selection accuracy typically drop, going from an 8-tool list to a 45-tool list, on tasks that only need one of the original 8?
contentSections.explanation: Published evaluations of tool-selection accuracy versus tool-count consistently show meaningful degradation well before 45 tools — often noticeable past 15-20, more pronounced past 40-50 — even when every added tool is individually well-documented. The mechanism isn't that any tool got worse; it's that every additional tool description is more context the model has to hold and compare against on every single decision, and more near-duplicate-sounding options increase the odds of picking a plausible-but-wrong one, the same failure mode from lesson two, just multiplied across more pairs.

contentSections.body:
This is a structural problem, not a writing problem — you cannot description-quality your way out of it. Every tool in the list is context the model re-reads and re-weighs on every single tool-selection decision, for the entire conversation, whether or not that tool is remotely relevant to the current step. A 60-tool list makes every decision, including the easy ones, marginally more expensive and marginally more error-prone, because "is this one of the right tools" now has 59 wrong answers to rule out instead of 7.

The honest cost here: this isn't free to fix either. Every mitigation in this lesson trades some complexity or some flexibility for reduced tool count at any one decision point — there's no version of this that's simply 'better' with no tradeoff.

A longer tool list degrades selection accuracy structurally, even when every individual description is good — because every added tool is more to compare against on every decision, not because any one tool got worse.

contentSections.title: The real fixes, and their real costs

contentSections.scenario:
An agent's 45-tool problem, and three approaches a team is considering.

**Approach A — grouping:** split into meta-tools like `manage_calendar(action, ...)` where `action` is an enum of sub-operations, cutting 12 calendar tools down to 1.

**Approach B — staged exposure:** only load the 6-8 tools relevant to the current task type into the model's tool list for that run, determined before the loop starts.

**Approach C — better descriptions:** keep all 45 tools, but rewrite every description to be more detailed and precise.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually addresses the structural problem from the first half of this lesson?

options.label: A and B
C — more precise descriptions is always the right lever
All three equally

feedback.ab: Right. Both A and B reduce the number of options actually competing for the model's attention at decision time — A by collapsing several tools into fewer with an internal enum choice, B by never showing irrelevant tools in the first place. Neither eliminates the underlying tradeoff (A adds a layer of indirection; B requires correctly predicting which tools a task needs before the run starts) but both attack the actual mechanism.
feedback.c: Better descriptions help with the lesson-one and lesson-two problems (ambiguity, misuse) but don't address *this* problem — the degradation here comes from sheer count, and 45 excellent descriptions still cost more attention to compare than 8 excellent descriptions. You can't write your way out of a quantity problem.
feedback.all: C alone, absent the other two, doesn't move the needle on count-driven degradation the way A and B do — see the explanation for the 'c' option. It's a good practice generally (module content from lessons 1-2) but not a fix for this specific failure mode.

contentSections.concept: The fixes that work are the ones that reduce how many tools are actually competing for attention at any one decision — either by collapsing several into one with sub-selection, or by not showing irrelevant ones at all for this particular run.

contentSections.body:
Both real fixes have a genuine cost, worth stating rather than glossing over. **Grouping** (`manage_calendar(action="create"|"delete"|"reschedule", ...)`) trades tool-count for schema complexity — you've moved the selection problem one level down, into choosing the right `action` value inside a single tool's schema, which is a smaller problem but not a zero one, and it makes each tool's schema and description longer and more branchy. **Staged exposure** (only load the tools relevant to this task type) trades tool-count for a prediction problem: something upstream now has to correctly guess which tool subset this run will need before the run has produced any information about what it actually needs, and getting that wrong means the agent hits a wall mid-task with a tool it needed but wasn't given.

Neither is free. Both are usually still worth it well before 45 tools, because the alternative — a flat, ever-growing list — is a cost that compounds silently on every single decision for as long as the agent exists, while the mitigation costs are paid once, at design time.

Grouping and staged exposure both cost something real — added schema complexity, or a prediction that can be wrong — but they attack the actual mechanism; rewriting descriptions, however well, doesn't fix a problem caused by count.

title: Rewrite eight bad tool definitions

title: Build a tool set an agent uses without errors
description: Design and test a small tool set for a real task, then run it enough times to have actual evidence — not a guess — about whether the model picks and calls the right tool correctly.

learningObjectives.text: Design a tool set of 3-5 tools with descriptions, schemas, and return values that avoid the failure modes from this module
Produce evidence, from real runs, of correct tool selection and argument construction

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: A tool set that looks right on paper and a tool set that's actually reliable are different things, and the only way to tell them apart is to run it enough times to see the failures a single glance at the code would never catch — this lab has you build one and get real evidence, not just a working demo run once.

contentSections.title: A small, reliable tool set
contentSections.brief: Pick a real small task with at least two plausible near-duplicate operations (e.g. a task-tracker agent with `create_task` and `update_task`, or a file-organizer agent with `move_file` and `rename_file`). Design 3-5 tools for it, using everything from this module: descriptions that name the boundary with neighboring tools, schemas with real constraints, return values that distinguish success/empty/failure. Then run the agent against 20 varied real prompts and log what actually happened.
contentSections.deliverable: The tool set's JSON definitions, the agent code that wires them up in a loop, a log of 20 runs with the prompt, the tool(s) called, and whether the call was correct, and a short written note on any run that failed and what you changed because of it.

stages.title: Design the tool set on paper first
stages.instructions: Before writing any code, write out the 3-5 tool definitions as JSON: name, description (using the four-part structure from lesson one), input_schema with real constraints (enum/required/pattern where they apply), and the shape of the return value for success, empty, and failure cases. For at least one pair of tools, deliberately write the boundary-naming sentence from lesson two into both descriptions.
stages.checkpoint: You have complete tool JSON for all 3-5 tools, and can point to the specific sentence in at least two descriptions that disambiguates them from each other.

stages.title: Wire it up and run it once, end to end
stages.instructions: Build the loop (from module 1's lab, or extend it) with these tools connected to real code — not stubs that just print. Run one prompt through it and confirm the whole path works: model calls a tool, your code executes it for real, the result comes back in a shape the model can act on.
stages.checkpoint: One complete, successful run, with a transcript showing a real tool call and a real result.

stages.title: Run 20 varied prompts and log every call
stages.instructions: Write 20 prompts covering the range of things this agent should handle, including at least 4 that are deliberately ambiguous between two of your tools (this is where lesson two's work gets tested for real). For each run, log: the prompt, which tool(s) got called, with what arguments, and whether that was the correct choice. Don't fix anything yet — just collect the evidence.
stages.checkpoint: A log of 20 runs with a clear correct/incorrect judgment on each one, including the ambiguous cases.

stages.title: Fix what the evidence shows, and re-verify
stages.instructions: For every incorrect call in your log, diagnose it using this module's categories — vague description, missing schema constraint, unresolved near-duplicate boundary, or unusable return value — and fix that specific tool. Re-run just the runs that failed to confirm the fix actually worked, and note in your write-up what you changed and why.
stages.checkpoint: Every previously-incorrect run now succeeds, and your write-up names the specific category of fix applied to each one — not a vague 'improved the prompt.'

rubric.criterion: Descriptions name the boundary with neighboring tools
rubric.meets: At least one pair of tools has descriptions that explicitly say when to use this one instead of the other, using a real decision criterion.

rubric.criterion: Schemas use real constraints, not just types
rubric.meets: At least one parameter uses enum, required, or a pattern/format constraint that meaningfully narrows valid input beyond 'is a string.'

rubric.criterion: Return values distinguish success, empty, and failure
rubric.meets: A tool call that finds nothing and a tool call that errors produce visibly different, distinguishable return shapes.

rubric.criterion: There's a real log of 20 runs, not a summary
rubric.meets: Each of the 20 runs is individually recorded with prompt, tool call, arguments, and a correct/incorrect judgment.

rubric.criterion: At least one real failure was found and fixed
rubric.meets: The log shows at least one genuinely incorrect tool call from the first pass, diagnosed to a specific cause, and confirmed fixed on re-run.

rubric.criterion: The fix write-up names a specific cause, not a vague improvement
rubric.meets: Each fix is tied to one of this module's specific failure categories (vague description, missing constraint, near-duplicate ambiguity, bad return shape).

contentSections.body: A tool set that's never been run 20 times against varied, deliberately ambiguous prompts hasn't actually been tested — it's just been read, and reading it is not the same evidence as watching it fail and fixing what you saw.

The only information channel the model has for deciding when and how to call this tool
An internal note that isn't sent to the model at all

The one specific wrong call a model would plausibly make with it, given how the task is likely to be phrased
The tool's internal implementation details

questions.from: This module — Tools

options.label: Makes an invalid value structurally impossible to send, not just discouraged in prose
Makes the tool call faster to execute
Tells the model which of the valid values is correct for the current situation

Note that an enum narrows to legal values, but — per option c, which is the tempting-but-wrong answer — it doesn't tell the model which legal value is the right one for this specific case; that's still the description's and the model's job.

None — the model will notice from context which case it is
It only matters for tools involving customer data

It doesn't degrade if every description is genuinely well-written

title: Stopping conditions you set, not ones it chooses
description: The difference between letting the model decide when a task is done and your code deciding, independently, when to stop believing it — and why relying only on the model's own end_turn is a design choice with a real failure mode, not a neutral default.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a model-owned stopping signal from a code-enforced one
Design a stopping condition that doesn't solely depend on the model reporting its own completion

contentSections.title: "I'm done" is a claim, not a fact

contentSections.body: An agent fixing a failing test suite runs `pytest`, sees three failures instead of the original five, writes "All tests are now passing" as its final text response, and stops — `stop_reason` reads `end_turn`, the loop exits cleanly, and the claim is false. Nothing in the loop's exit logic checked whether it was true.

contentSections.scenario:
Two loop-exit designs for the same test-fixing agent.

**A:**
```python
while True:
    response = call_model(messages)
    messages.append(response)
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break  # model says it's done
    ...
```

**B:**
```python
while True:
    response = call_model(messages)
    messages.append(response)
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        result = run_shell("pytest")
        if "failed" not in result and "error" not in result:
            break  # verified, not just claimed
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"Tests still failing:\n{result}"})
        continue
    ...
```
contentSections.question: Which one is exposed to the exact failure in the hook above — an agent that stops on a false claim of success?

options.label: A
B
Neither — both trust the model equally

feedback.a: Right. A treats `stop_reason != "tool_use"` as sufficient evidence the task is done — but that field only tells you the model chose to stop calling tools and write text. It says nothing about whether the text is true.
feedback.b: B doesn't take the model's word for it — it runs a real check (pytest, again) at the moment the model claims to be done, and only actually exits if that check confirms the claim. If the model is wrong, the loop keeps going with the real failure fed back in.
feedback.neither: A trusts the model's self-report completely — the only signal it checks is whether the model wants to keep calling tools, not whether what it's claiming is true. B adds an independent verification step precisely because that trust is misplaced often enough to matter.

contentSections.concept: `stop_reason` tells you the model stopped calling tools, not that the task succeeded. Those are different facts, and code that treats them as the same fact inherits every false-completion claim the model ever makes.

contentSections.body:
This is the loop-control version of module 1's model/code split: **whether to keep going is partly the model's call (it decides when it believes it's finished) and partly your code's call (it decides whether to believe that).** The mistake is collapsing these into one decision by treating `stop_reason != "tool_use"` as the entire stopping condition.

A stronger pattern, wherever the task has something checkable: when the model claims completion, run an independent verification — the actual test suite, the actual build, the actual linter — before honoring the claim. If verification fails, that failure becomes the next tool result, and the loop continues with real information instead of ending on an unverified claim. This isn't paranoia about the model lying; it's the same category of mistake as a person confidently reporting "fixed it" after a change they didn't actually re-test — usually not dishonest, just wrong, and worth catching the same way you'd catch it from a colleague: check, don't just believe.

`stop_reason != "tool_use"` tells you the model wants to stop, not that it should — wherever the task has something checkable, verify the claim before honoring it, and feed a failed verification back in as a reason to keep going.

contentSections.title: When there's nothing to verify against

contentSections.body: Not every task has a pytest to run. "Summarize this quarter's support tickets into three themes" has no automated check for "is this a good summary" — there's no exit code, no test suite, nothing to run that returns pass or fail. The verification pattern from the first pod needs a different backup here.

contentSections.scenario: An agent summarizing support tickets writes a three-paragraph summary, calls it done, and stops. There's no automated check available for whether it's actually a good summary.
contentSections.question: Given there's nothing to verify against, what's the actual design lever left for a stopping condition here?

options.label: A concrete, checkable rubric the model applies to its own output before claiming done — not free-form self-review, but specific criteria
There's nothing to do — accept the model's self-report as the only available signal
Run the same prompt three times and take a majority vote on whether each one seems done

feedback.rubric: Right. This is module 1's earlier point about vague self-critique loops resurfacing in a new place: 'is this a good summary' has no anchor, but 'does the summary name at least three distinct themes, cite a ticket count for each, and stay under 200 words' does — and the model checking itself against *that* is meaningfully more reliable than checking itself against nothing.
feedback.nothing: There's always something to tighten even without automation — the previous lesson's rubric point applies directly: a vague goal ('good summary') can be made into a checkable one ('three themes, each with a cited count') even when no code can automatically verify it.
feedback.vote: Running the same underlying judgment three times and voting doesn't introduce a new source of truth — it's the same self-assessment, sampled more times, which can catch genuinely random errors but does nothing for a systematic gap (e.g. the model consistently missing a theme category it doesn't recognize as one) that all three samples would share.

contentSections.mechanism: When there's no automated check available, the fix isn't giving up on verification — it's making the completion criteria concrete enough that even the model's own self-check has something real to measure against, rather than an open-ended 'is this good.'

contentSections.body: Two more code-owned backstops worth having regardless of whether verification is possible: a **required confirmation format** (the model's final answer has to include specific fields — "themes found: N" — that your code can check are present and well-formed before accepting the response as complete, catching the case where it stops with something that isn't even a real answer), and, as a last resort, a **human spot-check** on some percentage of runs, especially early on, to catch systematic problems no automated check would flag. None of these make the stopping decision fully code-owned the way `pytest`-verification does — for genuinely unverifiable tasks, you're narrowing the model's judgment call, not eliminating it, and that's an honest limit worth stating rather than pretending a rubric solves what only a real check can solve.

Without an automated check, you can't fully code-own the stopping decision — but a concrete rubric, a required output format your code validates, and periodic human spot-checks all narrow how much you're trusting an unverified claim, even when you can't eliminate the trust entirely.

title: Step limits, time limits and cost limits
description: Three different hard caps that stop a loop regardless of what the model wants, why they need to be different numbers for different reasons, and what a limit hit should actually do instead of just crashing.

learningObjectives.text: Set an appropriate step, time, and cost limit for a given agent task
Design what happens when a limit is hit, distinct from a normal success exit

contentSections.title: Three different caps, three different failure modes they catch

contentSections.body: An agent debugging a flaky test gets stuck in a pattern where it tries a fix, reruns, sees the same failure, tries a slightly different fix, reruns, and repeats — 40 iterations in, no step limit, no time limit, and by the time someone notices, it's made 40 real API calls and the conversation array is long enough that each subsequent call is measurably slower and more expensive than the last.

contentSections.scenario: Three separate agent runs on the same flaky-test-fixing task, none of them hitting a natural stop, each caught by a different limit: one at a step count, one at a wall-clock time, one at a dollar cost.
contentSections.question: For a task like this on a mid-size codebase, roughly how many tool-call iterations would a reasonable step limit allow before forcing a stop, if the task genuinely needs room to try 3-4 real hypotheses?
contentSections.explanation: A reasonable step limit gives real headroom above the expected case (a few iterations per hypothesis, times 3-4 hypotheses, is already 10-15) without being so generous it never actually catches a runaway loop. The exact number is less important than the principle: too tight and you cut off legitimate multi-hypothesis debugging early; too loose and the limit stops meaning anything, because a genuinely stuck loop will happily consume whatever headroom you give it.

contentSections.body:
Three limits, and they're not interchangeable — each catches a different failure:

**Step limit** (e.g. max 15 tool calls): catches a loop that keeps iterating without making real progress, regardless of how fast or cheap each iteration is. This is the one from the deploy-fix and test-fix examples across this phase — a loop that's technically calling tools correctly but not converging.

**Time limit** (e.g. max 5 minutes wall-clock): catches a loop that's slow for reasons unrelated to iteration count — a single tool call that hangs waiting on a slow external API, or a model response that takes unusually long. A step limit alone wouldn't catch this, because the loop might be sitting on iteration 3 of 15, well under the step cap, just stuck waiting.

**Cost limit** (e.g. max $2 of API spend): catches the case a step limit misses because not all iterations cost the same — module 1's point about the messages array growing every turn means iteration 15 of a run is far more expensive than iteration 1, since the whole history gets re-sent and re-billed each time. A run that's within its step limit can still blow past a reasonable budget purely because the conversation got long.

All three should generally be set, together, because each one is genuinely blind to the failure the other two catch.

Step, time, and cost limits each catch a different failure mode a runaway loop can hit — a loop that's technically progressing but slow, one that's fast but stuck, and one that's neither stuck nor slow but has simply gotten expensive as the conversation grew — so set all three, not just whichever is easiest to add.

contentSections.title: What happens when a limit is hit matters as much as the limit

contentSections.body: A step limit fires at iteration 15. The code does `sys.exit(1)`. Everything the agent had figured out — three ruled-out hypotheses, one partial fix already applied to a file — is gone, along with any way for a human picking this up to know what was already tried, and the next run (if there is one) starts from zero and probably repeats the same three dead ends.

contentSections.code:
while step_count < MAX_STEPS:
    response = call_model(messages)
    messages.append(response)
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = run_tools(response)
    messages.append(results)
    step_count += 1
else:
    print("Step limit reached, giving up.")
    sys.exit(1)
contentSections.question: This correctly enforces the step limit. What's still missing?

options.label: Anything useful for a human or a future run — what was tried, what was ruled out, what state the world is actually in now
The step limit should be a time limit instead
Nothing — the limit fires correctly and that's the whole job

feedback.context: Right. Firing the limit is necessary but not sufficient — a limit hit is exactly the moment you most need a record of what happened, because it means the task is genuinely hard or genuinely stuck, and that's valuable information to hand to whatever picks it up next (a human, or module 5's resumed run), not to discard.
feedback.wrong-limit: The limit type isn't the issue here — a time or cost limit would have the exact same problem if it also just printed a message and exited without preserving anything.
feedback.fine: Enforcing the cap correctly is real progress over no limit at all, but 'stopped safely' and 'stopped usefully' are different bars — this code clears the first and misses the second.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A limit hit should produce a structured record: what was tried (the last N tool calls and their results), what the current state actually is (did the last attempted fix get applied or not — this matters enormously for anyone picking it up), and an honest statement that the task didn't complete, distinguishable from a success exit. `sys.exit(1)` with a print statement throws all of that away at exactly the moment it's most needed.

contentSections.body: A limit hit should be its own distinct exit path — not a success, not a silent crash, but a labeled "stopped without finishing" state that preserves: the full message history up to that point (so nothing already discovered is lost), which limit fired and at what value, and ideally a short model-generated summary of what was tried and what's still unresolved, produced by one final call specifically asking for that summary rather than trying to task-complete. This last call is worth its small extra cost — a human reading "hit the 15-step limit, tried fixes A, B, and C, ruled out a config issue, still investigating whether it's a dependency version mismatch" can pick up productively in a way that "gave up" cannot.

A limit firing should produce a labeled, informative stop — what was tried, what's known, what's still open — not a bare exit, because the moment a limit fires is exactly the moment that information is most valuable and most likely to otherwise be thrown away.

title: Detecting a loop that's going nowhere
description: Recognizing the specific pattern of an agent stuck oscillating between the same few states — not just running long, but running long without making progress — and code-level ways to detect it before a step limit eventually catches it anyway, at greater cost.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a slow-but-progressing loop from one that's stuck repeating itself
Implement a repetition/progress check that detects a stuck loop earlier than a step limit alone would

contentSections.title: Long isn't the same as stuck

contentSections.body: Two twelve-iteration runs. In the first, the agent tried twelve genuinely different hypotheses for a bug, ruling each one out with real information, and is close to the actual cause by iteration twelve. In the second, the agent has called `run_shell("pytest")` seven times with byte-identical output each time, in between calling `read_file` on the same file it already read three times. Both hit the same step count. Only one is actually stuck.

contentSections.scenario: An agent debugging a bug has made 10 tool calls: read_file(app.py), run_shell(pytest), read_file(app.py), run_shell(pytest), read_file(app.py), run_shell(pytest)... alternating the same two calls with identical results each time.
contentSections.question: What specifically makes this a 'stuck' loop rather than just a long one?

options.label: The tool calls and their results are repeating without any new information entering the conversation
It has used more than 5 tool calls
It's using the same two tools instead of a wider variety

feedback.repeat: Right. The defining feature of stuck isn't the count or which tools are involved — it's that the same call is producing the same result, over and over, with nothing new for the model to actually reason from. A legitimately progressing loop can absolutely reuse the same two tools many times (read a file, run a test, read a different part of the file, run the test again) as long as each cycle turns up something new.
feedback.count: Count alone doesn't distinguish stuck from thorough — the good twelve-iteration run in the hook used just as many calls as the stuck one. A step limit catches both eventually, but at that point you've paid for the full stuck run before catching it, which is exactly what earlier detection avoids.
feedback.variety: Tool variety is a red herring — a legitimately progressing debugging session might reasonably alternate between exactly two tools (read, test) many times in a row if that's genuinely what the investigation calls for. The tell isn't which tools, it's whether the results are changing.

contentSections.mechanism: A stuck loop is defined by repetition without new information — the same call, the same result, cycling — not by its length or which tools it favors. Detecting that pattern catches the problem well before a length-based limit would, and at much lower cost.

contentSections.body:
A concrete detector: track the last few tool calls (name + arguments) and their results. If the same call-and-result pair (or a short cycle of 2-3 pairs) repeats more than a small threshold — say, three times — without any other call breaking the pattern, that's a strong stuck signal, independent of the overall step count. This is cheap to implement: a rolling window of the last 5-6 (call, result) pairs, checked for an exact or near-exact repeat, is enough to catch the pattern in the hook's example on its third repetition rather than its fifteenth.

Worth being honest about the limits of this detector too: it catches *literal* repetition well and *semantic* stagnation poorly — an agent trying five superficially different fixes that are all subtly wrong in the same underlying way (say, all patching a symptom rather than the actual root cause) won't trip a repeated-call detector at all, because every call and every result genuinely differs. That case needs a different signal, covered next.

Stuck means the same call and result repeating without new information — detect that pattern directly with a rolling window, rather than waiting for a step limit to eventually catch the same run at much higher cost.

contentSections.title: The subtler version: different calls, no real progress

contentSections.body: An agent tries five different fixes for a failing test, each one syntactically distinct — different file, different line, different approach — and every single one addresses a symptom ("the assertion is off by one") rather than the actual cause ("the loop that builds the list has an off-by-one in its range"). No repeated call anywhere in this transcript. It is still, in every sense that matters, stuck.

contentSections.problem: Design a progress check for the flaky-test-fixing agent that would catch the "five different symptom-patches, zero root-cause progress" pattern, since a repeated-call detector wouldn't see anything wrong here.

steps.label: Find the one signal that's actually not changing
steps.work: Across all five attempts, the same specific assertion (`assert result == expected`) is failing, at the same line, in the same test. The fix location changes; the failure signature doesn't.
steps.why: This is the thing to track instead of the calls themselves: not 'is the agent repeating an action' but 'is the actual problem it's fighting changing at all.'

steps.label: Define a concrete progress signal for this specific task
steps.work: For a test-fixing task: the specific failing assertion, or the specific error message/line number. Progress means this signature changes between attempts (even to a *different* failure — that's still evidence something moved) or resolves entirely.
steps.why: Different tasks need different progress signals — a code-review agent's progress signal might be 'number of files still unreviewed' instead. There's no universal one; it has to be defined per task type.

steps.label: Build the check: same failure signature across N attempts, flag it
steps.work: if failure_signature(attempt_5) == failure_signature(attempt_4) == failure_signature(attempt_3): flag_no_progress()
steps.why: This catches exactly the pattern the repeated-call detector missed — different actions, identical underlying obstacle, three times running.

steps.label: Decide what flagging actually does
steps.work: Not necessarily an immediate stop — often the better move is surfacing this to the model explicitly on the next turn: "Your last three fixes all addressed the same assertion failure without resolving it — consider whether you're treating a symptom rather than the root cause," then giving it one more attempt with that framing before escalating further.
steps.why: A no-progress flag is a strong hint the model itself can often act on productively, which is cheaper and more useful than immediately treating it as a hard stop.

faded.problem: Apply the same procedure to a code-review agent that's supposed to be working through a list of flagged files, but keeps re-flagging issues in files it already reviewed.

blanks.prompt: What signal isn't changing here, even though the specific tool calls (reviewing file X, then file Y, then file Z) look different each time?
blanks.answer: The set of files marked as fully reviewed isn't growing — it's re-visiting files already marked done instead of making progress through the unreviewed list.
accept: the count of newly-reviewed files stays flat / it revisits already-reviewed files

blanks.prompt: What's a concrete progress signal you could track for this task?
blanks.answer: The count (or set) of files marked reviewed-and-resolved, checked each turn for growth.
accept: number of files fully reviewed, should increase over time

blanks.prompt: What would the flag-and-nudge response look like here, mirroring the test-fixing example?
blanks.answer: Tell the model explicitly that it's re-reviewing already-completed files and ask it to move to the next unreviewed file in the list.
accept: surface the stagnation and redirect it to the actual remaining work

faded.why: The specific signal changes per task — assertion failures for test-fixing, reviewed-file count for code review — but the procedure is the same: find what should be moving if real progress is happening, and check whether it actually is.

contentSections.procedure: 1. Identify what 'real progress' concretely means for this specific task type. 2. Track that signal across iterations, not the raw call log. 3. Flag when the signal stalls for N consecutive iterations. 4. Prefer surfacing the stall to the model with an explicit nudge before escalating to a hard stop.

contentSections.body: A no-progress loop can look completely different on every turn and still be stuck — the fix is defining, per task, what real progress actually looks like and tracking that directly, not just watching for literal repetition.

title: Asking the human: when and how
description: Building a genuine pause-for-human-input point into the loop — not a blanket 'ask if unsure' instruction, but specific, code-recognized triggers and a interruption mechanism that actually halts execution rather than hoping the model remembers to wait.

learningObjectives.text: Identify concrete triggers that should pause an agent for human input, versus ones better handled by the model alone
Design a code-level mechanism that actually halts the loop for human input, not just a prompt instruction

contentSections.title: "Ask if you're not sure" doesn't work the way it sounds

contentSections.body: A system prompt says "if you're ever unsure whether an action is safe, ask the user first." An agent with a `run_shell` tool, mid-debugging-session, encounters a command it's about to run that would delete a directory — and doesn't ask, because from its own vantage point in that specific moment, it was confident, not unsure. The instruction relied on the model correctly self-assessing its own confidence at the exact moment that assessment mattered most, which is precisely the same failure shape as module 1's "only post if confident" example.

contentSections.scenario:
Two designs for when an agent pauses for human input.

**A:** System prompt: "If you're unsure about an action, especially a destructive one, ask the user before proceeding."

**B:** Code wraps every call to a tool tagged `requires_confirmation: true` (a small, explicit list — delete_file, run_shell with certain patterns, send_email to external addresses) with a hard pause: the tool call is not executed until a human explicitly approves it, and the loop cannot continue past that point without approval.
contentSections.question: Which design actually guarantees a human sees the risky action before it happens?

options.label: A
B

feedback.a: A depends entirely on the model correctly judging its own uncertainty in real time, on the specific action it's about to take — which is the same self-assessment reliability problem from module 1's confidence example. It will work often. 'Often' is not a guarantee.
feedback.b: Right. B doesn't ask the model to judge anything — it's a hard gate in the code, keyed off which specific tools are tagged, that mechanically blocks execution until a human acts. There's no point where the model's confidence, correctly or incorrectly assessed, is the thing standing between a risky action and it happening.

contentSections.concept: A human-in-the-loop checkpoint that depends on the model deciding to ask isn't a checkpoint — it's a request the model can, and eventually will, not make at the moment it matters most. A real checkpoint is a code-level gate the model cannot bypass regardless of what it believes.

contentSections.body:
Concrete, code-recognized triggers worth actually building, rather than the vague 'ask if unsure':

- **A tagged tool list** — specific tools (delete anything, send anything externally, spend money, modify anything in production) marked `requires_confirmation` at definition time, gated in code, not left to judgment.
- **A cost or scope threshold** — e.g. any single action affecting more than N records, or any run whose cumulative cost has crossed a set number, triggers a pause regardless of which specific tool it is.
- **A no-progress flag from lesson three** — genuinely stuck is a legitimate reason to hand control back rather than keep burning steps, and this is one of the few triggers where the model's own signal (it says it's unsure how to proceed) is reasonable to act on, because the cost of a false positive here is just a slightly premature human check-in, not an unrecoverable action.

Notice the pattern: the first two are triggers your code recognizes independent of the model's self-report, and only the third leans on the model's own signal, and only because that particular trigger's failure mode is cheap.

'Ask if unsure' asks the model to correctly notice its own uncertainty at the exact moment it matters — build hard, code-level gates on specific tools and thresholds instead, and reserve model-judgment triggers for the cases where a false positive only costs a premature check-in, not an action you can't undo.

contentSections.title: What "pause" has to actually mean in code

contentSections.body: A team builds a confirmation gate that works like this: the agent calls `delete_file`, the tool function prints "About to delete config.yml — continue? (y/n)" and calls `input()`. It works fine in a terminal, and falls over completely the moment the agent runs anywhere without an attached terminal to type into — a scheduled job, a Slack bot, a CI pipeline — because `input()` there just hangs forever, or crashes, with nobody around to answer it.

contentSections.scenario: A team is redesigning their confirmation-gate mechanism to work outside an interactive terminal — the agent runs as a scheduled job and needs to pause for a human who might respond minutes or hours later.
contentSections.question: Which of these are necessary parts of a confirmation gate that actually works in that environment?

items.label: The paused state (messages array, the pending tool call, everything needed to continue) gets persisted somewhere durable — not held only in an in-memory variable that dies if the process restarts
Something actively notifies a human that a decision is needed (a Slack message, an email) rather than the agent just waiting silently for someone to happen to check
A separate process can check whether a decision has been made and, if so, resume the exact paused state
The agent process itself should stay running and blocked on input() the whole time, to keep things simple
A timeout that decides what happens if no human responds within a reasonable window (escalate further, or fail safe by not proceeding)

explanation.persist: This is the module's central lesson-5 preview, arriving early: a pause that only exists in memory is a pause that vanishes the moment the process restarts, which is exactly the scenario a scheduled job or long-running service needs to survive.
explanation.notify: A gate nobody knows exists is not meaningfully different from no gate — if a human has to remember to go check on a paused agent with no prompt to do so, the pause could sit for days undiscovered.
explanation.poll: Since the process that hit the pause isn't necessarily the one that resumes it (module 5 covers this split fully), something needs a way to reload the saved state and continue from exactly where it left off, not from scratch.
explanation.sync: This is the input()-in-a-terminal design from the hook, which is precisely what breaks outside an interactive session — keeping the process blocked and synchronous is the thing that has to be abandoned to work in a scheduled/headless environment.
explanation.timeout: Real human response times vary from seconds to days; a pause with no timeout policy either blocks forever on an ignored notification or needs someone to remember it exists indefinitely — an explicit timeout with a defined fallback (escalate to someone else, or fail safe) closes that gap.

contentSections.synthesis: A confirmation gate that only works in a terminal isn't a general mechanism, it's a demo. A real one persists its state durably, actively notifies someone, allows resumption from a separate process, and has an explicit answer for silence — which is most of what module 5's resumability work needs anyway, so building this properly here isn't wasted effort.

contentSections.body: A pause that only works while a terminal is open and blocked on input() isn't a real human-in-the-loop mechanism — it needs to survive the process restarting, actively tell someone a decision is needed, and let a completely different process resume exactly where it stopped.

title: Resuming a run that stopped
description: What actually has to be saved for a stopped agent run — hit a limit, paused for a human, or crashed — to genuinely continue rather than restart, and the gap between 'looks resumable' and actually is.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the minimum state that must be persisted for a run to genuinely resume rather than restart
Implement a save/resume mechanism for an agent loop

contentSections.title: What "resume" actually requires

contentSections.body: An agent's process crashes at iteration 9 of a 20-step task. The team's "resume" logic reruns the original prompt from scratch. It's not resuming — it's restarting, and it pays for all 8 already-completed iterations again, in tokens and in any real-world side effects that aren't safely repeatable (a second email sent, a second file created with a slightly different name because a timestamp changed).

contentSections.scenario: The team's "resume" script takes the original task description and calls the agent loop again from an empty messages array. It's technically running again, but everything from the first 8 iterations is gone.
contentSections.question: What's actually missing for this to be a genuine resume rather than a restart in disguise?

options.label: The full messages array from the crashed run — without it, there's no way to continue from where the model actually was, only to begin again
A faster model, so the re-run completes quicker the second time
Better error handling so the crash doesn't happen at all

feedback.messages: Right. Per module 1's core point, the messages array *is* the entire state of the loop — nothing else needs saving for the model's side of things. Without it, the model has no memory of the 8 completed iterations, and the run isn't picking up where it left off, it's starting over with the same task description and none of the progress.
feedback.faster: Speed doesn't address the actual problem — a faster restart is still a restart, repeating 8 iterations of work (and any side effects) that had already genuinely happened.
feedback.prevent: Preventing every possible crash isn't realistic — processes get killed, machines reboot, deploys happen mid-run. The point of resumability is being able to recover gracefully when a crash happens anyway, not eliminating crashes.

contentSections.mechanism: The messages array is the complete state of an agent loop (module 1); persisting it, and reloading it before the next call, is the entire mechanism a real resume needs on the model side. Anything short of that is a restart wearing a resume's name.

contentSections.body:
The minimum viable resume: persist the messages array (to disk, a database row, anywhere durable) after every turn, not just at the end — a crash between turns should lose at most one turn's progress, not the whole run. On resume, load that array back and continue the loop exactly as if nothing had happened; the model has no way to tell the difference between a loop that ran continuously and one that was serialized, killed, and reloaded, because from its perspective the only thing that exists is the array it's handed.

One thing beyond the array itself needs care: **tool calls with real-world side effects that aren't idempotent.** If iteration 8 called `send_email` and the crash happened *after* the email genuinely sent but *before* the result got persisted to the saved state, a naive resume will re-run that same tool call and send a second email. This is the actual hard part of resumability, and it's worth being honest that it doesn't have a universally clean fix — the two real options are making tool calls idempotent where possible (a `create_ticket` tool that takes a client-generated idempotency key, so a retried call with the same key is a no-op) or persisting state *immediately* after a side-effecting call succeeds, before doing anything else, to shrink the crash window as small as it can go.

Resuming means reloading the exact messages array a crash interrupted, not rerunning the original task — and the one genuinely hard part is a side-effecting tool call whose result never got saved before the crash, which idempotency keys or tighter save timing narrow but don't fully solve for free.

contentSections.title: Resuming across a pause, not just a crash

contentSections.body: Lesson four's confirmation gate paused an agent for a human decision that might take minutes or might take two days. When the human finally responds, does the resumed run remember why it paused, or does someone have to manually reconstruct "oh right, this was the one about deleting the old branches"?

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order a proper pause-and-resume-for-human-input flow actually needs them, for lesson four's confirmation-gate scenario.
steps: Agent calls a tool tagged requires_confirmation; code intercepts the call before executing it
Full state is persisted: messages array, the specific pending tool call and its arguments, and a human-readable reason for the pause
A notification goes out to a human with enough context to decide without re-deriving it from scratch
Human responds (approve/reject), which is recorded against the persisted state, not just held in a chat thread
The process (possibly a different one than originally paused) loads the saved state, executes or skips the pending tool call based on the human's answer, and continues the loop
contentSections.explanation: The step people most often skip is persisting a human-readable reason alongside the raw state — without it, a human who responds two days later, in a different context, has to reconstruct why the pause happened from a bare tool-call JSON blob, which is exactly the situation lesson three's stuck-loop-summary and this lesson's crash-resume both already solved for a different scenario. The mechanism is the same each time: don't just save what to resume, save enough context that resuming doesn't require remembering.

contentSections.body: This closes the loop across all five lessons in this module: lesson one's verification, lesson two's labeled limit-stop, lesson three's stuck-loop summary, lesson four's confirmation gate, and this lesson's resume all rely on the same underlying discipline — treat every non-success exit from the loop as an event that needs to preserve enough state and enough context for whatever happens next (a human, a retry, a resumed process) to act on it without starting from zero. A stopping condition isn't just "decide when to stop" — it's "decide when to stop, and leave behind exactly what the next actor needs."

A resume, whether from a crash or a human pause, needs the same two things every time: the exact state to continue from, and enough context that continuing doesn't require anyone to remember or re-derive why it stopped in the first place.
