description: Seven real agent tasks. For each, decide the actual control policy: what limits, what verification, what human-gate triggers — with a specific reason, not a default 'add limits.'

learningObjectives.text: Design an appropriate control policy (limits, verification, human gates) for a described agent task

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Same underlying judgment call in seven different shapes: given a task, decide what actually needs a hard limit, what needs verification instead of trust, and what genuinely needs a human gate — versus what doesn't.
Control policy isn't a checklist you apply uniformly — it's matching the specific mechanism (limit, verification, human gate) to the specific failure it actually catches, task by task.

title: Add full loop control to your agent
description: Take the agent from modules 1-2's labs and add real, tested loop control: enforced limits with a labeled stop, stuck-loop detection, and a working resume from persisted state.

learningObjectives.text: Implement enforced step/time/cost limits with a distinct, informative stop path
Implement a stuck-loop detector and a working save/resume mechanism

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: The agent from modules 1-2's labs has no limits, no stuck-loop detection, and no way to resume from a crash — which means it's a demo, not something you'd trust to run unattended. This lab makes it something you actually would.

contentSections.title: Loop control, for real
contentSections.brief: Extend your agent (from module 1's hand-rolled loop, ideally with module 2's tool set) with three things this module covered: enforced limits that produce a labeled, informative stop instead of a crash or a silent success claim; a stuck-loop detector using either the repeated-call or no-progress pattern from lesson three; and a genuine save/resume mechanism you test by actually killing the process mid-run and resuming it from disk.
contentSections.deliverable: Updated agent code with all three mechanisms, a log showing at least one run that hit a limit and produced a labeled stop with useful context, a log showing the stuck-loop detector firing on a deliberately induced stuck case, and a transcript proving a real process-kill-and-resume worked (not a simulated one).

stages.title: Enforced limits with a labeled stop
stages.instructions: Add a step limit, a wall-clock time limit, and — if your API usage is trackable — a rough cost limit, all enforced in the loop itself, not left to the model. When any fires, don't just exit: make one final call asking the model to summarize what was tried and what's still unresolved, and save that alongside the full message history in a clearly labeled 'incomplete' state, distinguishable from a genuine success.
stages.checkpoint: A deliberately-hard task (or an artificially low limit) triggers the limit, and you have a saved record showing the labeled stop with a real summary, not a bare error.

stages.title: Stuck-loop detection
stages.instructions: Implement a rolling-window check for repeated (tool, arguments, result) triples, per lesson three. Test it by deliberately giving the agent a task it will genuinely get stuck on (an impossible or self-contradictory instruction is a reliable way to induce this) and confirm the detector fires before the step limit would have caught the same run.
stages.checkpoint: A log showing the detector firing on a real stuck run, at an iteration count clearly below your step limit — proving it caught the problem earlier than the limit alone would have.

stages.title: Save state every turn, and prove resume works by actually killing the process
stages.instructions: Persist the messages array to disk after every single turn (not just at the end). Start a real run on a multi-step task, and partway through — genuinely, from a separate terminal, with `kill` or equivalent — kill the process. Then write and run a separate resume script that loads the saved state and continues the loop. Confirm in the transcript that the model picks up with full context of what already happened, not starting over.
stages.checkpoint: A transcript that shows: the process actually being killed mid-run (not just stopped cleanly), and a subsequent resumed run whose first new model response clearly reflects awareness of the pre-kill history — not a restart from the original task description.

rubric.criterion: Limits are enforced in code, not requested in the prompt
rubric.meets: A test run with an artificially low limit demonstrably stops the loop regardless of what the model would otherwise do next.

rubric.criterion: A limit hit produces a labeled, informative stop
rubric.meets: The saved output of a limit-triggered stop includes a real summary of what was tried and is clearly distinguishable from a success completion.

rubric.criterion: The stuck-loop detector fires on a genuinely stuck run
rubric.meets: A deliberately induced stuck case triggers the detector at an iteration count below the step limit, proven with a real log.

rubric.criterion: Resume is proven against a real process kill, not a simulation
rubric.meets: The transcript shows an actual killed process and a separately-invoked resume that continues from saved state.

rubric.criterion: The resumed run demonstrably has the prior context
rubric.meets: The model's first response after resuming references or builds on something specific from before the kill, not a fresh start.

rubric.criterion: State is saved incrementally, not only at the end
rubric.meets: The save mechanism writes after each turn, so a kill mid-run loses at most one turn of progress, verifiable by checking the saved file's contents against where the kill happened.

contentSections.body: An agent you can trust to run unattended is defined by what happens when things go wrong — stuck, over budget, crashed — not by how well it performs on the happy path, which is exactly what this lab tested and the earlier labs didn't.

questions.prompt: `stop_reason != "tool_use"` tells you what, specifically?

options.label: The model chose to stop calling tools — not that the task was actually completed correctly
The task was verified complete

questions.from: This module — Controlling the Loop
questions.prompt: Why are step limits, time limits, and cost limits all needed together rather than just one of them?

They're redundant, but having all three provides a safety margin

questions.from: This module — Controlling the Loop
questions.prompt: What specifically defines a 'stuck' loop, as opposed to a long but genuinely progressing one?

options.label: The same call and result repeating, or the same underlying obstacle persisting, without new information entering the run
Using more than 10 tool calls
Repeatedly calling the same tool, regardless of the results

questions.from: This module — Controlling the Loop
questions.prompt: Why is 'ask the user if you're unsure' an unreliable human-in-the-loop mechanism on its own?

options.label: It depends on the model correctly judging its own uncertainty at the exact moment that judgment matters most
Users generally dislike being asked questions by an agent
It's fine on its own, and code-level gates are unnecessary

questions.from: This module — Controlling the Loop

options.label: The full messages array, since it's the entire state of the loop
Just the original task description
The model's weights and configuration

questions.explanation: Per module 1, the messages array is the complete state a loop has — reloading it and continuing is the whole mechanism a resume needs on the model side; the original task description alone reconstructs nothing about the 8 iterations of progress already made.

questions.prompt: What does an enum constraint in a JSON Schema actually prevent that a description alone cannot?

Makes the tool run faster

questions.prompt: What's the single property that makes a task agent-shaped rather than a fixed pipeline?

It uses more than one tool
It takes a long time to run

questions.explanation: This module's whole premise — that you can't know in advance how many iterations a debugging task will take — is a direct consequence of this earlier definition; loop control exists precisely because agent-shaped tasks don't have a knowable step count up front.

questions.prompt: If a wrong action would be expensive or irreversible, whose job is it to make that action impossible or gated?

options.label: Code — an enforced check, not the model's judgment alone
The system prompt, worded strongly
The model, since it usually judges correctly

questions.explanation: This is the exact principle behind this module's confirmation-gate design — a code-level gate on tagged tools, not a prompt instruction the model might not apply at the critical moment.

options.label: The model can't tell the two situations apart, because the return value itself destroyed the distinction
No real problem, as long as the model is careful
It only matters for financial data

title: What the model does when a tool errors
description: An error is just another message in the array — the model has no special channel for 'something went wrong,' which means how the error is worded determines how the model reacts to it, exactly like any other piece of text it reads.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a tool error is processed by the model the same way as any other tool result
Predict a model's likely next action given a specific error message's wording

contentSections.title: An error is a message, not an interrupt

contentSections.body: A `write_file` tool raises a `PermissionError` in your Python code. Your `except` block catches it, and somewhere in there a string gets built and appended to `messages` as a tool result. From that point on, as far as the model is concerned, there is no exception, no stack trace, no special "this went wrong" flag — there is only whatever string your code decided to put in that message, read the exact same way it reads a success result.

contentSections.scenario:
Two ways the same `PermissionError` gets turned into a tool result appended to `messages`.

**A:** `{"tool_result": "Error: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/etc/hosts'"}`

**B:** `{"tool_result": "Error"}`
contentSections.question: Both are technically 'an error was reported.' What's the actual functional difference to the model reading the next turn?

options.label: None — the model recognizes the word 'Error' either way and reacts appropriately
A gives the model concrete information (which file, why) it can reason from; B gives it nothing beyond 'something, somewhere, failed'
B is actually better because it's more concise

feedback.none: There's no special recognition happening — the model is reading text and generating a response based on that text, the same process either way. "Error" with no detail gives it exactly as much to work with as any other single word with no context.
feedback.info: Right. A tells the model exactly what happened (permission denied) and where (/etc/hosts) — enough to reason toward a real next step (try a path it has permission for, or recognize this needs elevated access it doesn't have). B gives it nothing to reason from beyond 'this failed,' which is exactly the situation that produces the guessing behavior from the next pod.
feedback.concise: Concise is a virtue when the content is still complete — B isn't concise, it's empty. There's no length at which "Error" contains the specific facts (which resource, which reason) a model needs to choose a sensible next move.

contentSections.concept: The model has no privileged channel for 'this is an error, treat it specially.' An error result is exactly as informative, or exactly as uninformative, as the string you put in it — nothing more.

contentSections.body:
This follows directly from module 1's core point in this phase: everything the model knows mid-run is what's in the `messages` array, and a tool error is appended to that array the same way a tool success is — as a `tool_result` block, read on the next turn like any other piece of text. There is no separate exception-handling pathway in the model's reasoning; "the tool errored" is not a fact the model has access to except through the words you chose to describe it with.

This has an uncomfortable consequence worth stating plainly: a badly-worded error message doesn't just fail to help — it actively misleads, because the model will construct a plausible interpretation of vague or misleading text exactly as confidently as it interprets clear text, with no internal signal distinguishing "I have enough information here" from "I am filling in gaps with a guess." A error message like `{"tool_result": "failed"}` after a `run_shell` call doesn't make the model cautious — it makes the model guess at what failed, and act on that guess with the same confidence it would act on a clear result.

A tool error is just a string appended to the array like any other tool result — the model has no separate 'this is an error, be careful' signal beyond what that string actually says, so a vague error produces a confident guess, not appropriate caution.

contentSections.title: Watching a vague error produce a wrong guess

contentSections.body: An agent calls `query_database("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4821")`. The tool result comes back: `{"error": "query failed"}`. The real cause was a connection timeout — nothing wrong with the query. The model's very next action: it rewrites the SQL, assuming the query itself was malformed, and tries again with slightly different syntax. It will keep doing this, plausibly, for as many iterations as it takes to either accidentally produce syntax the timeout doesn't interrupt, or exhaust a step limit.

contentSections.problem: Trace exactly why "query failed" leads the model toward rewriting the query, when the real problem was a connection timeout that has nothing to do with the query's correctness.

steps.label: The model reads the only information it has
steps.work: The tool_result says {"error": "query failed"}. That's the entire universe of facts available about what went wrong.
steps.why: No stack trace, no error code, no distinction between 'the SQL was invalid' and 'the connection dropped' exists anywhere in what the model can see.

steps.label: It has to form a hypothesis from that alone
steps.work: Given a database tool and the word 'query failed,' the single most available, most trained-on association is 'something about this query was wrong' — malformed syntax, a bad column name, a typo.
steps.why: This isn't the model being careless. Given genuinely no other information, 'the query itself is the problem' is a reasonable prior — it's just wrong in this specific case.

steps.label: It acts on that hypothesis
steps.work: It rewrites the SQL — maybe adjusting quoting, maybe simplifying the WHERE clause — and calls the tool again.
steps.why: This is a sensible action *given the hypothesis*. The hypothesis was wrong, but the reasoning from hypothesis to action was sound.

steps.label: The real cause never gets a chance to surface
steps.work: Because nothing in any tool result ever mentions a timeout, a connection, or a retry-worthy transient failure, the model has no path to the correct hypothesis, no matter how many syntax variations it tries.
steps.why: This is the actual cost of the vague error: not that the model reasoned badly, but that it was reasoning correctly from information that was missing the one fact that mattered.

faded.problem: Same scenario, but the error message is now: `{"error": "connection timeout after 30s — the query itself was not evaluated"}`. Trace what changes.

blanks.prompt: What's the first hypothesis the model would now form, given this specific wording?
blanks.answer: That the connection or network is the problem, not the query's syntax or content.
accept: a connectivity/timeout issue, not a bad query

blanks.prompt: What action follows naturally from that hypothesis — rewriting the query, or something else?
blanks.answer: Retrying the same query as-is, possibly after a brief pause, rather than changing it.
accept: retry unchanged, maybe with a delay, rather than rewrite the SQL

blanks.prompt: What single phrase in the error message is doing the most work to prevent the wrong hypothesis?
blanks.answer: 'The query itself was not evaluated' — explicitly ruling out the query as the cause.
accept: the query was not evaluated

faded.why: Nothing about the model's reasoning process changed between the two versions — only the information available to reason from did, and that alone was enough to point toward the correct next action instead of the wrong one.

contentSections.procedure: When diagnosing a wrong agent action after a tool error: don't ask 'why did the model reason badly' — ask 'what did the error message actually say, and was there enough information in it to distinguish the real cause from the most obvious wrong guess.'

contentSections.body: When an agent reacts wrongly to a failure, the useful diagnostic question usually isn't 'why did it reason badly' — it's 'what did the error message actually tell it, and did that leave room for the wrong guess to look like the best available hypothesis.'

title: Error messages written for the model to act on
description: A concrete template for a tool error that gives the model what it actually needs — what happened, why, and what to try instead — versus the raw exception text most tools return by default.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite a raw exception into a tool error the model can act on directly

contentSections.title: The four things a usable error message has

contentSections.body: The laziest possible error handling — `except Exception as e: return str(e)` — hands the model a raw Python traceback: `KeyError: 'customer_email'`. Technically true, technically informative to a Python developer who can go read the surrounding code. Useless to a model whose entire world is this one string, with no code to go inspect and no stack to walk.

contentSections.question: The model gets `{"error": "'customer_email'"}`. What's actually wrong with this, beyond just being terse?

options.label: It's a raw Python KeyError string with no context — not 'what field,' not 'why,' not 'what to try instead'
It should have raised the exception instead of catching it
Nothing — the model can infer the rest from the field name alone

feedback.raw: Right. `'customer_email'` alone is what Python prints when a dict lookup fails — it doesn't say 'the record has no email field,' doesn't say whether that's expected (maybe this customer opted out of email) or a real bug (maybe the column is actually named 'email' and the code has a typo), and doesn't suggest anything to try differently.
feedback.raise: Letting the raw exception propagate would crash the whole loop rather than give the model a chance to react at all — that's worse, not better. The problem here isn't that the exception was caught, it's that catching it produced a message with no useful content.
feedback.fine: The model can guess that something about 'customer_email' went wrong, but guessing what and why is exactly the failure mode from lesson one — a plausible guess isn't the same as correct information, and here there's a real, important distinction (bug vs. expected missing data) the message doesn't surface at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: `str(e)` on a `KeyError` reproduces exactly what a Python developer sees in a traceback, stripped of the traceback itself — no file, no line, no surrounding context, and critically, no interpretation. It's raw implementation detail leaking through as if it were a complete answer.

contentSections.body:
A usable error message has four things, and they map directly onto what the model needs to form a correct next hypothesis (lesson one):

1. **What was attempted** — restate the action in plain terms, since the model may be several turns removed from the original call by the time it reasons about the error.
2. **What actually happened** — the specific, real cause, translated out of implementation-speak. "KeyError: 'customer_email'" becomes "this customer record has no email address on file."
3. **Why, if knowable** — expected (this customer opted out) versus unexpected (this looks like a data problem) changes what the model should do next entirely.
4. **What to try instead, if there's an obvious next move** — not required, but often cheap to add and directly shortcuts the guessing lesson one described.

```python
except KeyError:
    return {
        "status": "error",
        "message": (
            "Could not retrieve email for customer 4821 — this customer's record "
            "has no email field, which usually means they opted out of email contact "
            "rather than a data error. Consider using their phone number instead, "
            "or ask the user how they'd like to proceed."
        ),
    }
```

This is the return-value design principle from the tools module (a status field that lets the model act differently on success vs. failure) applied specifically to the failure case, with the added requirement that the failure text itself be genuinely actionable, not just labeled as an error.

A usable error names what was attempted, what actually happened in plain language, why if it's knowable, and what to try instead if there's an obvious move — four things a raw exception string almost never has, because it was written for a developer with a stack trace, not a model with only this string.

contentSections.title: The cost of doing this for every tool

contentSections.body: Writing four-part error messages for every possible failure mode of every tool sounds like a lot of upfront work, and it is — the honest question is whether it's worth it, and the honest answer is: not uniformly. Some errors are worth this treatment and some genuinely aren't.

contentSections.scenario: A team has limited time and 12 tools, each with several possible failure modes. They're deciding where to invest in writing detailed, four-part error messages versus leaving a simpler generic message.
contentSections.question: Which of these failure modes justify the investment in a carefully written, specific error message?

items.label: A failure mode that occurs frequently in real usage (e.g. a rate limit that gets hit often)
A failure whose cause is genuinely ambiguous from the raw error alone, where a wrong guess is likely (the query-failed timeout example)
A failure that's extremely rare and, when it happens, is unambiguous even from a terse message (e.g. a malformed API key — there's really only one interpretation)
A failure where a wrong guess leads to a costly or hard-to-reverse next action

explanation.common: Frequent failures compound — a slightly-better error message on something that happens once in a thousand runs matters far less than one on something that happens once in ten.
explanation.ambiguous: This is exactly lesson one's timeout example — the entire value of a good error message is proportional to how much ambiguity it resolves. A message clarifying something already obvious adds little.
explanation.rare-obvious: If a terse message is already unambiguous (there's really only one plausible interpretation of 'invalid API key'), the four-part treatment adds writing effort without meaningfully changing what the model would have concluded anyway.
explanation.costly-guess: This is the highest-leverage category — even a moderately likely wrong guess is worth preventing if what follows from it is expensive, mirroring module 3's point about which decisions deserve the most enforcement.

contentSections.synthesis: The investment should track expected cost: frequency × ambiguity × how expensive a wrong guess would be. A rare, unambiguous, low-stakes error can keep a generic message. A common, ambiguous, or high-stakes one earns the full four-part treatment — this is a prioritization call, not a uniform standard applied everywhere.

contentSections.body: Writing a detailed, actionable error message for every possible failure isn't a realistic bar — prioritize the ones that are frequent, genuinely ambiguous, or where a wrong guess is expensive, and leave the rare, unambiguous, low-stakes ones with a simpler message.

title: Retry, change approach, or stop
description: The three responses to a tool failure, matched to the kind of failure it actually is — transient versus persistent, and within persistent, fixable-by-a-different-approach versus not — and why picking the wrong one of the three wastes a run or, worse, masks a real problem.

learningObjectives.text: Classify a tool failure as transient, approach-fixable, or unrecoverable, and match the response to it

contentSections.title: Three failures that look similar and aren't

contentSections.body: Three tool calls fail in the same run. One is a rate-limit response that will succeed if retried in 10 seconds. One is a malformed argument that will fail identically no matter how many times it's retried unchanged, but would succeed with a corrected argument. One is a permissions error that no retry, no rephrasing, and no amount of cleverness will fix — the agent genuinely does not have access, full stop. All three arrive as "the tool call failed." Only one of the three responses (retry, adjust, stop) is right for each.

contentSections.scenario: An agent's `run_shell` call fails three times in a row with the exact same error: `PermissionError: /etc/shadow`. Each time, the agent's response is to retry the identical command.
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with retrying here, mechanically?

options.label: A permissions error on a specific file doesn't change between retries — nothing about the situation is different the second or third time, so the outcome can't be either
The agent should retry with a longer delay between attempts
The command itself has a syntax error causing this

feedback.unchanged: Right. Retrying only makes sense when something about the situation might plausibly be different on the next attempt — a rate limit resets, a transient network blip clears, a lock released by another process. File permissions on /etc/shadow aren't going to spontaneously change between attempt one and attempt three of the same run; retrying here is pure waste, burning step budget on an outcome that was determined the instant the first attempt failed.
feedback.delay: A delay helps with genuinely transient failures (rate limits, momentary network issues) where time passing changes the outcome. It does nothing here, because the underlying cause — this process's permissions — isn't time-dependent at all.
feedback.syntax: A syntax error would typically produce a different, more specific error message (a shell parsing complaint), not a PermissionError, which is specifically about access rights, not command structure.

contentSections.mechanism: Retry only makes sense against a failure whose cause could plausibly be different on a later attempt. A permissions error is a fact about the current situation that doesn't change with time or repetition — retrying it is confusing 'try again' with 'this might work differently next time,' which for this specific cause, it won't.

contentSections.body:
Three categories, and the response that actually fits each:

**Transient** — the cause is time-dependent and plausibly different on a later attempt: a rate limit, a momentary network blip, a lock held by another process that's likely to release. **Response: retry**, ideally with a short backoff, and a cap on how many times (an unlimited retry is its own version of the stuck loop from module 3).

**Approach-fixable** — the cause is a mistake in *this specific attempt* that a different attempt could avoid: a malformed argument, a wrong assumption about a file's location, a query using the wrong column name. **Response: change the approach** — different arguments, a different tool, more information gathered first — not a bare retry of the identical call, which would just fail identically again.

**Unrecoverable** — the cause is a fact about the environment that no retry or clever rephrasing changes: missing permissions, a resource that genuinely doesn't exist, a hard business-logic rule ("refunds over $500 require manager approval" and no manager-approval tool exists). **Response: stop and report clearly** — this maps directly to module 3's labeled-stop design, because pretending a genuinely blocked task might resolve with more tries wastes the run and delays the honest report that it's actually stuck.

The skill worth building is fast, correct classification — not memorizing the three categories, but reading a specific failure and correctly placing it, because the same-looking "tool call failed" message can be any of the three.

Retry fits a cause that's plausibly different next time; changing approach fits a mistake in this specific attempt; stopping fits a fact about the environment that no retry or rephrasing touches — and correctly telling these three apart, fast, matters more than knowing the categories exist.

contentSections.title: Building the classification into the error message itself

contentSections.body: Rather than hoping the model correctly infers which of the three categories a failure belongs to from context alone, the error message can just say — and this is cheap, because your code, catching the specific exception type, usually already knows which category it's dealing with better than the model has to guess.

contentSections.problem: Redesign a `call_external_api` tool's error handling to communicate the retry/adjust/stop category explicitly, for the three failure types this tool actually sees: rate limits (429), bad request (400), and authentication failure (401).

steps.label: Rate limit (429) → transient, retry
steps.work: {"status": "error", "category": "transient", "message": "Rate limited — retry after roughly 30 seconds. This is not a problem with your request.", "retry_after_seconds": 30}
steps.why: The code catching this specific status code already knows, with certainty, that this is transient — there's no reason to make the model infer that from a bare '429' when the exact category and even a wait time are known facts your code has.

steps.label: Bad request (400) → approach-fixable, adjust
steps.work: {"status": "error", "category": "fix_and_retry", "message": "Request rejected: 'customer_id' must be numeric, got 'CUST-4821'. Strip the prefix and retry with the numeric portion only."}
steps.why: Not just 'bad request' — the specific field, the specific problem, and the specific fix, because a 400 usually does carry a real, parseable reason in the response body that's worth surfacing rather than discarding.

steps.label: Authentication failure (401) → unrecoverable at this level, stop
steps.work: {"status": "error", "category": "unrecoverable", "message": "Authentication failed — the API key is invalid or expired. This requires a human to update the credentials; no retry or different request will succeed."}
steps.why: This explicitly rules out both retry and rephrasing, which is exactly the information that prevents the model from burning several turns trying variations on a call that was never going to work regardless of its content.

steps.label: Make the category machine-readable, not just prose
steps.work: The `category` field (transient / fix_and_retry / unrecoverable) is there for your loop's own control logic too — e.g. auto-capping retries on `transient` failures, or immediately triggering module 3's labeled stop on `unrecoverable` ones — not just for the model to read.
steps.why: The same signal that helps the model decide can also drive code-level control logic, which is more reliable than hoping the model always makes the code's job for it by reasoning its way to the right response every time.

faded.problem: Apply the same three-case design to a `deploy_service` tool that can fail with: a build timeout (genuinely transient — the build server was momentarily overloaded), an invalid config file (a mistake in the deploy request itself), or a frozen deployment window (a hard organizational policy — no deploys between 5pm Friday and 9am Monday, no exceptions).

blanks.prompt: What category and response fits the build timeout?
blanks.answer: Transient — retry, likely with a short backoff, since an overloaded build server may well succeed shortly after.
accept: transient, retry

blanks.prompt: What category and response fits the invalid config file?
blanks.answer: Approach-fixable — identify and correct the specific config problem, then retry with the corrected file, not a bare retry of the same broken config.
accept: fix_and_retry, correct the config then retry

blanks.prompt: What category and response fits the frozen deployment window?
blanks.answer: Unrecoverable within this run — no retry or config fix changes a hard policy window; stop and report that the deploy must wait or be manually approved.
accept: unrecoverable, stop and report

faded.why: The procedure doesn't change with the domain — identify whether the cause is time-dependent, fixable-by-a-different-attempt, or a fixed fact, and write the error message (and the code-readable category) to say so explicitly rather than making the model reverse-engineer it.

contentSections.procedure: For each known failure mode of a tool: (1) determine whether your code already knows the category (transient/fixable/unrecoverable) at the point it catches the error, (2) if so, state that category explicitly in both a machine-readable field and plain language, (3) for fixable failures, name the specific fix; for unrecoverable ones, explicitly rule out retry and rephrasing so the model doesn't waste turns trying either.

contentSections.body: Your code usually already knows which of the three categories a failure belongs to, at the exact moment it catches the error — say so explicitly, in a field the loop's own control logic can use and in plain language the model can act on, rather than making the model guess at a classification your code already has.

title: The agent that reports success after a failure
description: The specific, dangerous failure mode of an agent that claims a task completed when a step silently failed partway through — how it happens mechanically, and why it's worse than an honest failure report.

learningObjectives.text: Trace how a silent partial failure produces a confident false-success report
Design a check that catches a partial failure before the agent reports overall success

contentSections.title: How a false 'success' actually gets produced

contentSections.body: An agent tasked with updating 50 customer records reports: "Done — updated all 50 records." In fact, record 31 failed silently (a validation error the tool swallowed and returned as `{"updated": false}` without the agent noticing the field), and the agent's final summary was generated from its own memory of having *attempted* 50 updates, not from actually checking the 50 results for which ones succeeded.

contentSections.scenario: The agent called update_record 50 times, one of which returned {"updated": false, "reason": "validation failed"}. Its final message said all 50 succeeded.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that produced this false claim?

options.label: The model summarized based on having attempted 50 calls, not on having verified 50 individual results — 'I called update 50 times' got conflated with '50 updates succeeded'
The model is lying to make itself look more competent
The tool result format is fine — this is purely a model reasoning failure

feedback.conflate: Right. Across 50 tool calls and 50 results, the model's summary is built from its overall sense of the run, and 'I made 50 calls, mostly successful' can get compressed into 'all 50 succeeded' without a deliberate check that actually counts successes against the total — it's a rounding-off of the attempt count into a completion claim, not a deliberate falsehood.
feedback.lying: There's no mechanism by which the model would benefit from claiming false success, and nothing about how these models are trained rewards confident fabrication over accurate reporting. The much more mundane and much more common explanation is a summarization failure, not deception.
feedback.fine-format: A result format that returned {"updated": false, ...} did communicate the failure correctly at the individual-call level — the gap is between that individual signal and the final summary, which is exactly why the fix in this lesson is a code-level count-and-verify step, not just a better per-call result format (which this scenario already has).

contentSections.mechanism: Across many tool calls, a model's final summary is a compression of everything that happened — and compression can silently drop a single dissenting result among 49 successes unless something forces an explicit count-and-check rather than a general impression.

contentSections.body: This is the single most dangerous version of the model/code split from module 1: the claim "the task succeeded" is exactly the kind of thing that's expensive to get wrong (someone acts on the false belief that all 50 records are correct) and exactly the kind of thing a model's own summary is unreliable at, once the number of individual results grows past what fits cleanly into a confident one-line claim. It's not a comprehension failure on any single result — the model correctly read `{"updated": false}` when it happened. It's an aggregation failure: forty-nine correct individual reads compressing into one incorrect overall claim.

A false success claim after a batch of calls usually isn't a single wrong read — it's forty-nine correct reads and one silent one, compressed into a summary that rounds off the dissent, which is exactly the aggregation step a model's own narrative summary is worst at doing reliably.

contentSections.title: The fix is a count, not a better prompt

contentSections.body: "Please make sure to accurately report if any updates failed" is a request the model will genuinely try to honor and still get wrong on run 31 out of 40, for the same reason a careful person, hand-tallying fifty outcomes from memory at the end of a long task, would also occasionally round off the one exception. The fix that actually works doesn't ask the model to try harder at counting.

contentSections.scenario: A team is fixing the 50-record-update agent to stop making false success claims.
contentSections.question: Which of these would actually prevent the specific failure — not just reduce its odds through better wording?

items.label: Code-level accounting: track every individual result as it comes back, and have code — not the model's summary — construct the final report from the actual count of successes and failures
The loop's own stopping condition checks the count before allowing an 'all succeeded' exit — if any recorded failure exists, the loop cannot report full success
A stronger prompt instruction: 'Double-check your work and be completely honest about any failures'
Having the model re-read all 50 raw results in a dedicated final step specifically to count successes and failures, rather than summarizing from general memory of the run

explanation.code-count: This removes the model from the counting step entirely — your code already has every individual result and can compute the true count deterministically, which is strictly more reliable than any model-generated summary, the same way module 1's argument-schema constraints were strictly more reliable than a prompt request.
explanation.block: This is module 3's stopping-condition-verification lesson applied here directly: don't let the loop exit on a success claim without an independent check confirming it — here, checking the actual tallied results before the claim is allowed to stand.
explanation.prompt: A stronger instruction asks the same summarization process, that already compressed 49-successes-and-1-failure into 'all succeeded,' to somehow do a better job next time through sheer effort. It doesn't change the actual mechanism (a narrative summary compressing many individual facts) that caused the error.
explanation.final-review: This is a genuine improvement over summarizing from memory of the whole run, because it forces the model to look at all 50 raw results again in a focused pass — closer to code-level counting in spirit, though a deterministic code count is still more reliable than even a careful model re-read.

contentSections.synthesis: The strongest fix removes the counting from the model's judgment entirely — code tallies the real results and constructs the report, or at minimum gates the success claim on that tally. A model re-reading everything specifically to count is a real improvement over a memory-based summary; a stronger prompt instruction alone is not, because it doesn't change the underlying mechanism that produced the error.

contentSections.body: The fix for a false-success claim isn't asking the model to be more careful — it's removing the counting from the model's summary entirely, letting code tally the real results and gate any 'succeeded' claim on that tally matching reality.

title: Failing loudly and usefully
description: What a genuinely useful failure report looks like — for a human debugging it later, and for module 3's resume mechanism picking it up — versus a stack trace, a silent log line, or a vague 'something went wrong.'

learningObjectives.text: Design a failure report that gives a human everything needed to act, without requiring them to reconstruct context

contentSections.title: Loud doesn't mean alarming — it means findable and complete

contentSections.body: An agent hits an unrecoverable failure at 2am, logs `ERROR: task failed` to a file nobody's watching, and exits. Nobody finds out until a customer complains three days later that their request never got processed, and the person investigating then has to reconstruct, from scratch, what the agent was even trying to do — because "task failed" is genuinely all the log contains.

contentSections.scenario: The agent's failure was technically logged — the log line exists, in a file, on disk. Nobody found out for three days, and when they did, the log line was nearly useless.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap between 'logged' and 'failed loudly and usefully,' here?

options.label: Two separate things: nothing actively surfaced the failure to a human, and the log content itself had no reconstructable context even for someone who did look
The log level should have been WARNING instead of ERROR
Nothing — logging the failure was the correct behavior, the team just wasn't watching closely enough

feedback.both: Right, and both gaps need fixing separately. A failure nobody's notified about might as well not be logged (module 3's confirmation-gate lesson made this same point about a pause nobody's told about). And separately, a log line with no context — no task description, no what-was-attempted, no what's-actually-broken — costs whoever eventually reads it real time reconstructing what should have been captured at the moment of failure, when all the relevant facts were still in memory.
feedback.level: Log level is a minor mechanical detail next to the two structural problems: nobody was actively told, and the content wouldn't have helped much even if they'd looked immediately.
feedback.watching: Expecting a human to proactively monitor a log file for a rare failure is exactly the kind of passive-notification failure this lesson (and module 3's confirmation-gate lesson) argues against — the system should push the notification, not assume someone's watching.

contentSections.mechanism: A failure that's technically recorded but neither actively surfaced nor genuinely reconstructable from what was recorded has satisfied the letter of 'log the error' while missing the actual point of failing loudly, which is that someone finds out promptly and can act without redoing the investigation from zero.

contentSections.body:
A genuinely useful failure report has the same shape module 3 built for limit-hits and human-gate pauses, because it's solving the same underlying problem: **what does the next actor — human or resumed process — need, so they don't have to reconstruct what already happened?**

- **What the task was** — the original request, not assumed to be remembered by whoever's reading this later.
- **What was attempted** — the specific sequence of actions taken before the failure, not just the final one.
- **What actually broke, specifically** — using lesson two's four-part error structure, not a bare exception string.
- **Current state** — critically, whether anything partially completed (echoing lesson four: don't let "it failed" hide that 30 of 50 records did get updated before it broke).
- **Active notification** — pushed to wherever a human will actually see it promptly, not left for someone to find.

This isn't a new idea introduced at the end of the module — it's module 3's labeled-stop pattern, applied specifically to the unrecoverable-failure branch of lesson three's retry/adjust/stop decision, closing the loop on everything this module has covered.

A useful failure report answers what was attempted, what specifically broke, and what state things are actually in right now — pushed actively to someone who'll see it, not left in a log file for someone to eventually stumble onto.

contentSections.title: Putting the whole module together
A batch job goes wrong at 3am
contentSections.opening: Your agent processes a nightly batch of 200 invoice-reconciliation tasks. It's currently running. At task 147, the payment-processor API starts returning 503s intermittently — sometimes succeeding, sometimes failing, no clear pattern. You're the one who gets paged.

classify.situation: The 503s are inconsistent — not every call fails, and the ones that do fail sometimes succeed on an immediate retry. This is happening mid-run, live.
classify.question: Using lesson three's three categories, what is this failure, and what should the running agent's response be?

choices.label: Transient — retry with a short backoff and a cap, keep processing the batch
choices.consequence: This matches the actual pattern (inconsistent, sometimes-immediate-retry-succeeds) — the agent retries failed calls with backoff, most succeed on retry within a couple of attempts, and the batch continues with a handful of tasks taking slightly longer.

choices.label: Treat every 503 as unrecoverable and stop the whole batch immediately
choices.consequence: This overreacts to a pattern that's actually intermittent and often self-resolving on retry — you've now stopped 53 legitimate remaining tasks because of a transient issue that a bounded retry would likely have handled.

midbatch.situation: The batch continues. At task 189, the 503s stop being intermittent and become constant — every single call now fails the same way. The retry-with-backoff logic has been dutifully retrying and failing for the last 6 tasks with zero successes.
midbatch.question: What should change now?

choices.label: Keep applying the same transient-failure retry logic — it worked for the first 147 tasks
choices.consequence: Six consecutive identical failures with zero successes is a different pattern than the earlier intermittent one — this now looks like module 3's stuck-loop signal (same call, same result, repeating) layered on top of the retry logic, and continuing to retry burns budget on a cause that's stopped being transient.

choices.label: Recognize the pattern has changed — six consecutive identical failures is evidence this is no longer transient — stop the batch and produce a labeled failure report
choices.consequence: The agent stops cleanly, and its failure report states: 188 of 200 invoices reconciled successfully, tasks 189-200 blocked by what now appears to be a sustained payment-processor outage (constant 503s since task 189, not intermittent), with the specific invoice IDs still pending listed explicitly.

overreacted.summary: Correctly avoided a false-success claim, but misclassified a genuinely transient pattern as unrecoverable and stopped 53 tasks that a bounded retry would likely have completed.
overreacted.lesson: Classification has to match the actual pattern observed, not default to the most cautious category — over-cautious stopping has a real cost too, just a less dramatic one than a false success.

burned-budget.summary: The retry logic that correctly handled the first 147 tasks kept running unchanged after the failure pattern genuinely changed, burning budget on a cause that had stopped being transient without ever recognizing the shift.
burned-budget.lesson: A classification made once at the start of a batch isn't permanent — the same failure signature repeating identically, per module 3's stuck-loop detection, is itself new evidence that should trigger reclassification, not just more retries.

handled-well.summary: The agent adapted its classification as the evidence changed, stopped cleanly rather than either false-claiming success or silently grinding on a dead cause, and produced a report specific enough that a human could pick up exactly where it stopped.
handled-well.lesson: The three responses from lesson three aren't a one-time decision at the top of a task — they're a continuous read of the evidence, and a pattern shifting from intermittent to constant is itself the signal that the right response has changed too.

contentSections.body: The retry/adjust/stop classification isn't a single decision made once — it has to keep tracking the actual evidence as a run continues, because a pattern that starts transient can become sustained, and treating an early classification as permanent is its own version of the stuck-loop problem.

title: Design error handling for eight tool failures
description: Eight real tool failure scenarios. For each, classify it (transient/fixable/unrecoverable) and design the response — not a generic 'handle the error' but the specific message and action this failure calls for.

learningObjectives.text: Classify a tool failure and design an appropriate, specific response

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Same judgment call in eight shapes: read the failure, classify it correctly, and name the response that actually fits — not a default retry, not a default stop.
Fast, correct classification is the actual skill here — the three categories are simple to list and easy to misapply under real, ambiguous-looking failures.

title: Make your agent survive a hostile tool layer
description: Deliberately break your agent's tools — random failures, malformed responses, slow responses — and build the error handling that makes it complete or fail honestly instead of confabulating a false success.

learningObjectives.text: Implement error-message design, retry/adjust/stop classification, and false-success prevention against a genuinely unreliable tool layer

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every tool in your agent so far has probably worked correctly almost all the time in testing, which tells you almost nothing about how it behaves under real-world flakiness. This lab makes your tools actively hostile on purpose, so you can find out.

contentSections.title: Surviving unreliable tools
contentSections.brief: Take your agent (from earlier labs in this phase) and wrap its tools in a deliberate failure layer: a configurable percentage of calls randomly return a transient-style error (simulate a rate limit or timeout), a smaller percentage return a genuinely unrecoverable error (simulate a permissions failure), and — this is the important one — make it possible for a batch-style task to have some sub-operations silently fail while others succeed, so you can test lesson four's false-success problem directly.
contentSections.deliverable: The failure-injection wrapper, updated tool error messages using lesson two's four-part structure with an explicit transient/fixable/unrecoverable category, retry logic with a cap for transient failures, a code-level tally that gates any success claim on a real count, and a log of at least 3 full runs showing the agent correctly surviving injected transient failures, correctly stopping on an injected unrecoverable one, and correctly reporting a partial success rather than a false full success.

stages.title: Build the failure-injection layer
stages.instructions: Wrap your existing tools so that, based on a configurable probability, a call raises a simulated transient error (rate-limit-style, recoverable on retry) or a simulated unrecoverable error (permissions-style, never recoverable). For any multi-call/batch-style tool use in your agent, make it possible for individual sub-calls to fail independently, so some succeed and some don't within the same task.
stages.checkpoint: Running your existing agent unmodified against the wrapped tools now produces visible failures — confirming the injection layer actually works before you build anything to handle it.

stages.title: Rewrite error messages and add retry/stop classification
stages.instructions: For each injected failure type, rewrite the tool's error response using lesson two's four-part structure (what was attempted, what happened, why, what to try), with an explicit category field. Add loop logic that retries transient failures a bounded number of times with backoff, and immediately produces module 3's labeled stop on an unrecoverable one, without further attempts.
stages.checkpoint: A run with only transient failures injected completes successfully after visible retries; a run with an unrecoverable failure injected stops cleanly with a labeled report, not a crash or an endless retry.

stages.title: Fix the false-success problem for real
stages.instructions: Run a batch-style task against the injection layer configured so a handful of sub-operations fail silently among many successes. Confirm — before making any fix — that your agent currently reports full success incorrectly. Then implement lesson four's fix: a code-level tally of actual results that gates the final report, so a partial failure is always reported as partial, never rounded up to complete.
stages.checkpoint: A before/after comparison: a logged run showing the unfixed agent falsely claiming full success on a batch with real injected failures, and a logged run after the fix correctly reporting the true count of successes and failures.

rubric.criterion: Failures are genuinely injected, not simulated in the write-up only
rubric.meets: The failure-injection wrapper actually runs and actually causes real tool calls to fail at the configured rate, verifiable in a log.

rubric.criterion: Error messages follow the four-part structure with an explicit category
rubric.meets: At least two rewritten error messages, one transient and one unrecoverable, show what/what happened/why/what-to-try plus a machine-readable category field.

rubric.criterion: Transient failures are retried with a cap, not endlessly
rubric.meets: A log shows bounded retry attempts (not one, not unlimited) on an injected transient failure, succeeding after backoff.

rubric.criterion: Unrecoverable failures stop immediately with no wasted retries
rubric.meets: A log shows zero retry attempts on an injected unrecoverable failure, immediately producing a labeled stop.

rubric.criterion: The false-success bug is demonstrated before being fixed
rubric.meets: A before-fix run log exists showing the agent incorrectly claiming full success on a batch with real injected partial failures.

rubric.criterion: The fix is a real code-level tally, not a prompt change
rubric.meets: The after-fix report's success/failure counts are traceable to code that counted actual tool results, not to a reworded instruction to the model.

contentSections.body: An agent that's only ever been run against tools that work is untested in the one dimension that actually matters for something you'd trust unattended — this lab is the first time in the phase your agent has had to prove it fails honestly, not just succeeds cleanly.

title: Checkpoint — Errors Inside the Loop
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from loop control, 2 from further back.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's error-handling design, and reconnect it to loop control and agent-loop fundamentals

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Errors Inside the Loop
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.from: This module — Errors Inside the Loop
questions.prompt: Why does a vague error message ('failed') cause a confident wrong guess rather than appropriate caution?

options.label: The model has no separate 'this is uncertain, be careful' channel — it forms a hypothesis from whatever text it has, with the same confidence regardless of how little information that text contains
The model doesn't recognize the word 'error' reliably
It doesn't — vague and detailed errors produce equally good outcomes

questions.explanation: This is the module's opening mechanism — an error is a string like any other, and a string with little information produces a guess with the same apparent confidence as one built from a genuinely informative message.

questions.from: This module — Errors Inside the Loop
questions.prompt: What are the four elements of a genuinely usable error message?

options.label: What was attempted, what actually happened, why if knowable, what to try instead
Error code, timestamp, stack trace, severity level
The raw exception text, verbatim

questions.explanation: A stack trace and error code are exactly the raw-exception-style content the lesson argues is written for a developer with code to inspect, not a model with only the string in front of it.

questions.from: This module — Errors Inside the Loop
questions.prompt: A permissions error, retried three times with the identical result each time — what's the correct classification and response?

options.label: Unrecoverable — stop and report; the cause isn't time-dependent so retrying can't change the outcome
Transient — keep retrying with backoff
Approach-fixable — try slightly different arguments

questions.explanation: A permissions fact about the current environment doesn't change with time or repetition, which is exactly what distinguishes unrecoverable from transient — retrying wastes budget on an outcome that was already determined.

questions.from: This module — Errors Inside the Loop
questions.prompt: A batch of 50 tool calls has one silent failure among 49 successes, and the model's summary claims full success. What's the actual mechanism behind this, and the real fix?

options.label: A summarization/aggregation failure — the fix is a code-level tally that gates the success claim, not a stronger prompt asking for more care
The model deliberately misrepresented the outcome
A stronger system-prompt instruction to double-check reliably fixes this

questions.explanation: The model read each individual result correctly — the failure is in compressing 50 results into one summary claim, which a prompt instruction doesn't fix because it doesn't change the underlying compression mechanism; only removing the counting from the model's judgment does.

questions.from: This module — Errors Inside the Loop
questions.prompt: What makes a failure report 'loud and useful' rather than just logged?

options.label: It's actively pushed to someone who'll see it promptly, and contains enough context (what was attempted, what broke, current partial state) that they don't have to reconstruct it themselves
It uses the ERROR log level rather than WARNING
It's written in more alarming language

questions.explanation: This mirrors module 3's labeled-stop and confirmation-gate patterns directly — a record that's technically written down but neither actively surfaced nor reconstructable fails the actual point of failing loudly.

questions.from: Previous module — Controlling the Loop
questions.prompt: What's the minimum state that has to persist for a crashed agent run to genuinely resume rather than restart?

options.label: The full messages array
Just the original task description
The model's configuration settings

questions.explanation: Relevant again here — this module's failure reports are exactly the kind of state a resumed run, or a human picking up a failed task, needs preserved alongside (or instead of) a full crash resume.

questions.from: Previous module — Controlling the Loop
questions.prompt: What specifically defines a 'stuck' loop rather than a long but genuinely progressing one?

options.label: The same call and result, or the same underlying obstacle, repeating without new information
Using more than some fixed number of tool calls
Repeatedly calling the same tool

questions.explanation: This is exactly the pattern in this module's 3am case-sim, where six identical failures in a row was the signal that a transient classification needed to be revisited — the same repeated-result detection, applied to failure classification instead of general progress.

questions.from: Previous module — Controlling the Loop
questions.prompt: Why is 'ask the user if you're unsure' an unreliable human-gate mechanism on its own?

options.label: It depends on the model correctly judging its own uncertainty at the exact moment that judgment matters most
Users generally don't want to be asked
It works fine without a code-level gate

questions.explanation: The same self-assessment-reliability problem shows up in this module too — a model correctly recognizing 'this failure means I should stop' is exactly the kind of judgment call worth backing with a code-level rule (the category field), not just hoping it notices.

questions.from: Older module — Tools
questions.prompt: A tool result that can't distinguish 'nothing found' from 'the lookup failed' causes what problem?

options.label: The model can't tell the two situations apart, because the return value itself destroyed the distinction
No real problem if the model reads carefully
It only matters for tools involving money

questions.explanation: This is the direct ancestor of this module's whole premise — good error design is what happens when you take that same 'the return value has to distinguish real cases' principle and apply it specifically to the failure branch.

questions.from: Older module — What an Agent Actually Is
questions.prompt: If a wrong outcome would be expensive, whose job is it to prevent it — the model's judgment, or an enforced check?

options.label: An enforced check in code
The model's judgment, since it's usually reliable
A more strongly worded prompt instruction

questions.explanation: This module's false-success fix (a code-level tally gating the claim) is this exact principle from the very first module of the phase, applied to what might be the single most consequential judgment call an agent makes: whether to report that it succeeded.

contentSections.body: If the false-success question felt like the hardest one to hold onto, that tracks — it's the module's central case, and it's worth re-reading lesson four once more before the final module, which builds a real agent where this exact mistake would be easy to make invisibly.
